title: 8 Reel Scripts
section: REM Academy — 8 Reel Scripts (from Posts & Emails)
text:
8 Reel Scripts › REM Academy — 8 Reel Scripts (from Posts & Emails)

Eight you-to-camera reels, each pulled straight from a post or email you've already put out — same ideas, same voice, now in talking-head form. Filmed at the desk, on-brand (dark teal + emerald), blunt and calm. Talk to **one person**. Speak in positives — never exclude anyone (new shooters, working pros, and agency owners are all welcome).

> **These are NEW** — they don't repeat the existing REM Academy - 7 Reel Scripts (What is REM / curriculum / what you're missing / the $20–30K skill / why me+founding / guest speakers / zero speed ramps). Film both sets in the same look and you've got a 15-reel run into July 15.

**Where each one comes from:**

| # | Reel | Source |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 3,000,000 views — no trends, no AI | "Views" post + email *"How I got 3,000,000 views"* |
| 2 | You don't need mansions | "You Don't Need Mansions" post (the $2,500 condo) |
| 3 | The cheapest clients are the most frustrating | "Cheap Clients" post |
| 4 | The math most solo shooters get wrong | email *"The Math Most Solo Shooters Get Wrong"* |
| 5 | They're reading you before frame one | "5 Things Clients Notice" post |
| 6 | One agent who rebooks > ten one-offs | email *"One agent who rebooks you > ten one-offs"* |
| 7 | "Isn't this saturated?" | Carousel idea #4 (objection crusher) |
| 8 | I built an AI that critiques your photos | Critique Bot post + email |

**How to read these:** every reel gives you **2–3 hook reads** (film all of them — the hook makes or breaks the reel), the **spoken script** (know the beats, *talk* it, don't read it word-for-word), **on-screen text**, and **b-roll**. Pause between beats so the editor has clean cut points.

title: 8 Reel Scripts
section: REEL 1 — "3,000,000 views, no trends, no AI"
text:
8 Reel Scripts › REEL 1 — "3,000,000 views, no trends, no AI"

**~60s · Job:** prove you understand attention, then hand over the system. Wide top-of-funnel.

**Hook (film all):**
- "My real estate content's done about three million views. No trends, no AI, no posting five times a day. Let me show you the whole system."
- "Everyone thinks going viral is luck. It's not — it's boring, and it's repeatable. Here's exactly what I do."

**Script:**
> My real estate content has done about three million views. One photo did sixty-five thousand. One reel hit 1.6 million.
>
> No trends. No AI. No posting five times a day to feed the algorithm.
>
> Everyone thinks virality is luck. It's not — it's a system, and honestly, it's boring in the best way.
>
> Here it is. Three posts a week. Monday — your single best photo from a recent listing. Proof you can shoot. Wednesday — a short behind-the-scenes of how you got that shot. Friday — you, talking to camera. One strong take, one tip. That last one breaks out for me almost every time.
>
> Win the first second, every time — motion or a spoken hook, never a logo. Reply to every comment in the first hour. And use the collab feature so one post hits two feeds.
>
> That's it. Good work, posted consistently. You don't have to game the algorithm — you just have to give it something worth watching.
>
> That's the part we go deep on inside REM Academy. Comment "REM" and I'll send you the details.

**On-screen text:** "~3,000,000 views" · "no trends · no AI · no posting 5x a day" · "Mon: the work / Wed: the process / Fri: the take" · "Win the first second" · "comment REM"
**B-roll:** screen-record of your analytics (the 65.9K photo, the 1.6M reel); thumb scrolling your feed; you filming a talking-head; a collab post showing on two accounts.

title: 8 Reel Scripts
text:
8 Reel Scripts › REEL 2 — "You don't need mansions"

**~55s · Job:** kill the "my market is too small" excuse with a real story + number. Story-driven, high saves.

**Hook (film all):**
- "You don't need to shoot mansions to charge a lot. Every shot in this video is a dated condo — and that shoot was twenty-five hundred bucks."
- "I get this DM every week: 'the houses in my market don't look like yours.' It's backwards — let me show you."

**Script:**
> I get some version of this DM almost every week. "What do I do — the houses in my market don't look like yours. Obviously you can charge a lot, you're out there shooting Montecito mansions."
>
> I get it. But it's backwards.
>
> Every shot I'm showing you right now is the same listing. A condo. The kitchen still has its original maroon cabinets — hasn't been touched in years. Not a mansion in sight.
>
> That shoot was twenty-five hundred dollars. Photos and one simple video.
>
> The price didn't come from the property. It came from how it was shot — and how I show up before I ever raise the camera. Same eye, same standard, same systems, whether it's a dated condo or an oceanfront estate.
>
> Your market isn't the ceiling on what you can charge. Your standard is.
>
> So stop blaming your market. Start raising your standard.
>
> That's exactly what I teach inside REM Academy. Comment "MARKET" and I'll send you the details.

**On-screen text:** "Every shot = the SAME listing" · "A dated condo. $2,500." · "Your market isn't the ceiling. Your standard is." · "comment MARKET"
**B-roll:** the actual condo set (the maroon kitchen → the polished finals); a hard cut to a Montecito estate for contrast; you working the condo like it's a $40M home.

title: 8 Reel Scripts
section: REEL 3 — "The cheapest clients are the most frustrating"
text:
8 Reel Scripts › REEL 3 — "The cheapest clients are the most frustrating"

**~50s · Job:** relatable pain → the positioning reframe. Hits every shooter who's been burned by a lowball client.

**Hook (film all):**
- "The cheapest clients are almost always the most frustrating ones. Here's why — and what I do now."
- "I used to drop my price to 'help' people out. Every single time, it backfired."

**Script:**
> The cheapest clients are almost always the most frustrating ones.
>
> It's not that they're bad people. It's that the smallest budgets come with the biggest expectations. Every detail gets questioned, a simple job turns into a hard one, and the math never works out in your favor.
>
> For a while I tried to help by dropping my price. Every time, I just shrank my own margin and worked twice as hard to justify it. So now I hold firm — and honestly, the work and the relationship are both better for it.
>
> Here's the part nobody tells you: you don't earn premium prices by asking for them. You earn them by how you're positioned.
>
> When you're known as the best in your market — offering something your competition can't, delivering top-tier every single time — a higher fee stops being a question. It becomes obvious.
>
> That's exactly what I teach inside REM Academy: how to position yourself at the top of your market and charge like it.
>
> Comment "COHORT" and I'll send you the details.

**On-screen text:** "Cheapest client = biggest headache" · "You don't earn premium by asking — you earn it by positioning" · "Hold firm." · "comment COHORT"
**B-roll:** you calm and unbothered on a call; premium delivery / a clean gallery handoff; a booked-out calendar.

title: 8 Reel Scripts
section: REEL 4 — "The math most solo shooters get wrong"
text:
8 Reel Scripts › REEL 4 — "The math most solo shooters get wrong"

**~60s · Job:** break the "you have to build an agency" belief + show the real ceiling. Pair it with your revenue screenshot.

**Hook (film all):**
- "Most solo shooters are capping their own income and don't even know it. Here's the math they get wrong."
- "You don't need to build an agency to make real money in this. One person can do fifty, sixty grand in a month."

**Script:**
> Most solo shooters are quietly capping their own income without realizing it.
>
> There's this belief that to make real money in real estate media you have to build an agency — hire shooters, take on overhead, become a manager instead of a creative. I believed it too, for a while.
>
> It's not true.
>
> The shooters earning the most aren't the ones with the biggest teams or the fanciest gear. They're the ones who price properly and offer the full package an agent actually needs to sell a home — not "shoot, deliver, get out."
>
> Get that combination right, and one person can do fifty, sixty grand in a single month. No team. No payroll. No overhead eating it alive.
>
> I know how that sounds — so here's a recent week, just me. *(show the screenshot)* And that was before a single forty-seven-hundred-dollar invoice, for one shoot, even hit.
>
> That's not a flex. It's the point. The ceiling is so much higher than someone charging two-fifty a listing thinks it is.
>
> That's exactly what REM Academy is built on. Comment "REM" and I'll send you the details.

**On-screen text:** "You don't need an agency." · "One person · $50–60K/month" · "It's not team size. It's pricing + package." · "comment REM"
**B-roll:** your Stripe / revenue screenshot (the recent week, the $4,750 invoice); you working a shoot solo; a quick "no team / no payroll" text beat.
**Note:** drop in your *real* number for that week so it stays honest — the script leaves a clean spot for the screenshot.

text:

**~50s · Job:** the soft-skill edge nobody teaches. Builds you as the substance guy and is very re-watchable.

>
> How you walked into the listing. Whether you listened, or just waited to pitch. How you handled the first bit of pushback. Whether you needed the booking, or could walk away.
>
> None of it is scripted. All of it is felt.
>
> The job doesn't start when you raise the camera. It starts the second you walk in the door.
>
> And the photographers who stay booked aren't always the most technical. They're the ones who show up calm, certain, and clearly worth it. Your energy sets the price before your portfolio ever does.
>
> That's the part nobody teaches. We do, inside REM Academy.
>
> Comment "REM" and I'll send you the details.

**On-screen text:** "They're reading you before frame one" · "Listened, or waited to pitch?" · "Calm. Certain. Worth it." · "Your energy sets the price." · "comment REM"

title: 8 Reel Scripts
section: REEL 6 — "One agent who rebooks > ten one-offs"
text:
8 Reel Scripts › REEL 6 — "One agent who rebooks > ten one-offs"

**~55s · Job:** recurring revenue — REM's core promise. The fix for feast-or-famine.

**Hook (film all):**
- "One agent who rebooks you every month beats ten one-time clients. It's not even close."
- "Anyone can land one shoot. Here's how you stop starting back at zero every single month."

**Script:**
> Anyone can land one shoot. The real money is in the rebook.
>
> One agent who books you every month is worth more than ten one-time clients you have to find, chase, and convince all over again.
>
> Here's how you turn a single shoot into a monthly client. Be the easy button — give them the full package so they never have to call three different people. Deliver fast, and deliver the same quality every time, so they never have to wonder what they're getting. And book the next one before you even leave the driveway.
>
> Do that with five to eight agents, and you've got a real business — predictable bookings, predictable income. And happy agents talk. They refer you. That's free top of funnel.
>
> So stop hunting for the next client. Start keeping the ones you've already got.
>
> That's exactly what we build inside REM Academy. Comment "REM" and I'll send you the details.

**On-screen text:** "The money's in the rebook." · "1 monthly agent > 10 one-offs" · "Be the easy button · same quality every time · book the next before you leave" · "comment REM"
**B-roll:** a calendar filling up with the *same* names; you handing over a gallery; booking the next shoot on the spot at the door.

title: 8 Reel Scripts
text:
8 Reel Scripts › REEL 7 — "Isn't this saturated?"

**~50s · Job:** crush the #1 excuse for staying out. Reframes the market as wide open at the top.

**Hook (film all):**
- "'Isn't real estate media saturated?' It's the number-one excuse keeping people out — and it's wrong."
- "Everyone tells me this market's too crowded. From the outside, sure. Up close, it's wide open."

**Script:**
> "Isn't real estate media saturated?"
>
> It's the number-one excuse keeping people out of a skill that quietly pays twenty to thirty grand a month. And it's wrong.
>
> From the outside, yeah — it looks crowded. A flood of people with cameras and a Sunday-afternoon rate. That's what you see.
>
> But here's the truth: it's saturated with cheap. It's starving for good.
>
> Flaky, inconsistent, amateur — that's most of the market. Reliable and premium is rare. And every city has agents who genuinely can't find anyone good they can trust on a two-million-dollar listing.
>
> That seat — the premium one — is wide open. The crowd's all down at the bottom fighting over scraps.
>
> So don't ask if it's saturated. Ask if you're willing to be the one agents can actually count on.
>
> That's exactly what REM Academy builds. Comment "REM" and I'll send you the details.

**On-screen text:** "'Isn't it saturated?'" · "Saturated with cheap. Starving for good." · "The premium seat is wide open." · "comment REM"
**B-roll:** a fast montage of generic listings / a crowd of cameras → hard cut to your premium work; a $2M+ listing; an agent shaking your hand.

title: 8 Reel Scripts
section: REEL 8 — "I built an AI that critiques your photos"
text:
8 Reel Scripts › REEL 8 — "I built an AI that critiques your photos"

**~60s · Job:** show the Critique Bot as a real, tangible reason to join. Demo-driven.

**Hook (film all):**
- "I built an AI that critiques your real estate photos. You upload a shot — it tells you the truth."
- "When you shoot solo, nobody catches the leaning verticals or the color cast. So I built something that does."

**Script:**
> When you shoot solo, there's nobody to catch the leaning verticals, the color cast, or the angle that quietly flattens the room. The agent just says "looks great," and you're left guessing whether your work is actually MLS-ready — or quietly costing you the next booking.
>
> So I built a fix. It's an AI critique tool, trained on the exact standards I use to shoot forty-million-dollar listings.
>
> You drop in any property photo, and in seconds it scores it one to ten across the ten things that actually matter — verticals, perspective, composition, exposure, color, light, edit craft. Then it hands you a ranked list of what to fix: what to reshoot, what to correct in post, and the small polish that separates a good photo from a portfolio one.
>
> No inflated grades. Seven is MLS-ready. Nine-plus is portfolio. And you can run a whole shoot through it — up to thirty-five photos — and it'll tell you how consistent your set actually is.
>
> It's the feedback loop that takes years to build with a mentor… in seconds. And it lives inside REM Academy.
>
> Comment "BOT" and I'll send you everything.

**On-screen text:** "An AI that critiques your photos" · "Scored 1–10 · ranked fixes" · "🔴 reshoot · 🟡 post · 🟢 polish" · "7 = MLS-ready · 9+ = portfolio" · "comment BOT"
**B-roll:** screen-record of the bot scoring a real photo; the ranked fix list appearing; gallery mode reading a full set; you at the desk uploading a shot.

title: Editing SOP
text:
Editing SOP › REM Editing SOP (v1, 8/24)

Drafted from Call 11 (How I Edit) + Shoot Masterclass calls, for the Call 11 replay post (Daniel's ask: the mandatory steps, for team/editor handoff). **Files:** `~/JG Terminal/REM Academy/Editing SOP/REM Editing SOP.pdf` (3-page emerald-branded, attach to Skool) + `REM Editing SOP.md` (editable source — the FULL content lives there; this note is the operational summary + pointers).

**The locked sequence:** 0) frame stack in capture order (window pull → ambient ~2 stops under flash WB → front flash 45° ISO 400 1/8 → directional pops → outside umbrella ~1/4 → safety window frame; blown frame fix order: power→ISO→shutter) · 1) Lightroom: preset all, edit WINDOW frame first + 5-star, ambient auto-WB-then-warm, copy/paste onto flash frames + re-fix WB, open as layers · 2) Photoshop: Reverse Layers action, pick base frame, per-layer Camera Raw, mask shooter (flow 6–14%), local masks over global opacity (competing shadows), umbrella-frame window spill, interior flash frame = window pull (skip safety frame), Blend Ambient Luminosity 25–35% · 3) Mandatory finish: merge → cleanup (discretionary) → cinematic green ~6% → merge → Unsharp Mask 40–45% → Cmd+S · 4) LR polish: 6+P, highlights up, matte curve, HSL sanity, guided-transform verticals.

title: Twilight Masterclass
text:
Twilight Masterclass › 1. Cold-open hook  *(0:00–0:20)*

**[OPEN FULL-FRAME on the finished twilight money shot — warm windows, deep blue sky. Hold 2 sec. Cut to Jacob standing in front of the same house at dusk, camera on tripod beside him, lights glowing behind.]**

> This image right here? This is the difference between a three-hundred-dollar shoot and a listing package an agent will pay thousands for.

> It's the photo that goes on the cover. It's the one that stops the scroll. And by the end of this masterclass, you're going to know exactly how to make it — start to finish, on a real listing, with me.

**[Beat. Smile.]**

> Let's get into it.

**[CUT TO: REM v2 intro card — emerald/ink, Space Grotesk: "THE TWILIGHT MASTERCLASS."]**

---

title: Twilight Masterclass
section: 2. Intro — who I am + why twilight is the money shot  *(0:20–1:30)*
text:
Twilight Masterclass › 2. Intro — who I am + why twilight is the money shot  *(0:20–1:30)*

**[ON CAMERA, in front of the house, golden light still up.]**

> Quick intro if we haven't met — I'm Jacob. I shoot luxury real estate in Santa Barbara and Montecito, I've photographed homes north of forty million dollars, and I've put media on over five billion dollars in listings. And I'm telling you that not to flex — I'm telling you so you know the stuff I'm about to teach you is the exact same stuff I get paid premium money to do.

> So here's the truth about twilight photos. Most photographers treat them as an add-on. A "nice to have." A box you check.

> They're not. The twilight is the **money shot**. It's the single most valuable image you can hand an agent. A warm, glowing home against a deep blue sky — that's not a photo of a house, that's a feeling. That's "I want to live there." That's the image that makes a buyer book the showing.

**[Gesture to the house behind you.]**

> And the best part? It is way more learnable than it looks. It's not talent. It's timing, a couple of settings, and a process. That's all it is. And today I'm going to give you the whole thing.

---

title: Twilight Masterclass
text:
Twilight Masterclass › 3. What you'll walk away with  *(1:30–2:10)*

**[ON CAMERA.]**

> Here's the plan. This is filmed in three parts.

> Right now — this video — we're doing the setup. The part nobody films. Showing up while it's still light, reading the house, prepping it, and locking in our shots *before* the good light ever hits. This is where the shot is actually won or lost.

> Next video, we shoot. You're going to stand right next to me while the light drops and watch me work the window in real time.

> And in the last video, we take the frames we just captured and I edit the hero shot start to finish — so you see the whole thing, camera to final image.

> Nothing held back. Let's start with the most important thing nobody talks about — timing.

---

title: Twilight Masterclass
section: 4. Why timing is everything — the blue-hour window  *(2:10–3:30)*
text:
Twilight Masterclass › 4. Why timing is everything — the blue-hour window  *(2:10–3:30)*

**[B-ROLL: sky overhead, the sun getting low. Jacob checking a sun/blue-hour app on his phone.]**

> Twilight is not a time of day. It's a window. And it's short — you've got maybe twenty, thirty minutes of truly great light, and the best of it is more like ten.

> The magic happens right after the sun drops below the horizon. The sky's still holding color — that deep blue, sometimes a little pink or orange left over — but it's dark enough that the lights inside the house actually *glow*.

> That balance is the whole game. There's a moment where the brightness of the sky and the brightness of the windows are almost even. That's your shot. That's the money.

**[Hold up phone showing the times.]**

> Too early, and the sky's too bright — the windows look flat, no glow, no magic. Too late, and the sky goes black — now it just looks like a photo taken at night, no depth, no separation. You miss it by ten minutes in either direction and you've got a mediocre photo.

> So I pull up a sun app, I find my sunset time, and I know my window opens right around there and closes fast. Which is exactly why we're here over an hour early — because once that light shows up, there is zero time to think.

---

title: Twilight Masterclass
text:
Twilight Masterclass › 5. Reading the house & the sun  *(3:30–4:45)*

**[WALKING the property with the camera, gesturing at the house and the sky.]**

> First thing I do when I get to any twilight: I figure out where the color's going to be, and which face of the house I'm shooting.

> The sun's setting over there. So the richest color in the sky — that warm-to-blue gradient — is going to build on that side and wrap overhead. I want that color *in my frame*, behind or above the house, doing the work for me.

**[Point at the front elevation.]**

> Now look at the house. This front elevation faces the right way, it's got great glass, and those windows are going to read like lanterns once the lights are on. That's my hero. That's the shot the agent's going to lead with.

> I'm also looking at the practical stuff — where can I put a tripod, what's in the way, where are the ugly distractions. Power lines, a neighbor's trash can, a parked car. I clock all of it now, in the daylight, while I can still do something about it.

---

title: Twilight Masterclass
section: 6. The gear (and why it's less than you think)  *(4:45–6:00)*
text:
Twilight Masterclass › 6. The gear (and why it's less than you think)  *(4:45–6:00)*

**[B-ROLL: laying out the kit — body, tripod, the lenses, drone in the case.]**

> Let's talk gear, because this is where people overcomplicate it and waste money. My whole philosophy is the least gear for the best quality. Here's literally everything I use for a twilight.

> A camera body. Any modern one is more than enough.

> A **tripod**. This is non-negotiable for twilight. We're shooting long exposures in low light — if that camera moves, the shot's soft, it's done. The tripod is doing real work tonight.

**[Hold up the tilt-shift.]**

> My hero lens is a **24-millimeter tilt-shift**. Wide enough to get the whole home, and the tilt-shift lets me keep all my vertical lines perfectly straight — the house stands up tall and correct, no leaning walls. That "architectural" look? That's a lot of it right there. You don't have to own one to start — a regular wide lens works, you'll just straighten in post.

**[Hold up the zoom.]**

> Then a **24 to 70** for handheld creative angles — shooting through landscaping, catching a reflection in the pool, tighter detail shots.

**[Gesture to drone.]**

> And a **drone**, for when the light's good and the property earns an elevated hero. That's it. That's the kit. No giant lighting setup, no crew. The light does the work — our job is to be ready for it.

---

title: Twilight Masterclass
section: 7. Scouting your compositions before the light moves  *(6:00–7:30)*
text:
Twilight Masterclass › 7. Scouting your compositions before the light moves  *(6:00–7:30)*

**[Jacob setting the tripod at the hero position, looking through the camera, B-roll over his shoulder of the framing.]**

> Okay, this is the step that separates pros from everyone else. I lock in my compositions *now*, in daylight, while I have all the time in the world. When the light hits, I'm not composing — I'm just clicking.

> So I walk the property and I find my three or four angles. The hero — the wide, straight-on, lead-the-listing shot, right here. Then a three-quarter angle to show some depth. Maybe the back of the house with the pool. Maybe a tight one of the entry glowing.

**[Look through viewfinder, adjust.]**

> For the hero, I'm getting low-ish, I'm leveling the camera, I'm making sure my verticals are dead straight, and I'm framing so the sky has room to do its thing up top. I'll lock the tripod right here and leave it.

> Pre-visualize every shot before the light comes. Know your sequence. Because in twenty minutes, all of this thinking has to already be done.

---

title: Twilight Masterclass
section: 8. Prepping the home — lights, glass, staging, clutter  *(7:30–9:30)*
text:
Twilight Masterclass › 8. Prepping the home — lights, glass, staging, clutter  *(7:30–9:30)*

**[B-ROLL: Jacob walking through the home turning on every light, a montage. Then outside, adjusting things.]**

> Now the part that makes the glow — prepping the house. And you want this fully done *before* the light turns, because once it's go-time you can't be running inside flipping switches.

> Rule one: **every light on.** Every single one. Interior lamps, overheads, under-cabinet lighting, the entry, the exterior sconces, landscape lighting, pathway lights, pool light, spa. If it makes light, it's on. That's what fills those windows.

**[At a window, adjusting blinds.]**

> Glass — I want the glow to escape. So blinds open, or sometimes I'll close a sheer for a soft, even glow. It's a judgment call per window, but the goal is warm light reading through the glass, not a dark hole.

**[Outside, moving a hose / straightening.]**

> Then I stage the exterior like it's a magazine cover. Cars out of the driveway. Trash cans hidden. Hose coiled or gone. Cushions straightened. Turn on the fire feature if there is one — fire reads incredible at twilight. Pool and spa on. And inside, TV off, or a nice still image on it.

> Spend your daylight here. A clean, fully-lit home shot at the wrong time still beats a cluttered, half-dark home shot at the perfect time. Do both right and it's unbeatable.

---

title: Twilight Masterclass
text:
Twilight Masterclass › 9. Setting up the hero frame  *(9:30–10:30)*

**[Jacob behind the locked-off tripod, dialing in.]**

> Last thing before we wait for the light — I get the hero frame fully set on the tripod so it's ready to fire.

> Camera's level, verticals are straight, composition's locked. I'll set my base exposure now and just fine-tune it as the sky drops. I'm shooting RAW, manual mode, low ISO, and I'll explain every one of those numbers in the next video when we're actually pulling the trigger.

**[Step back, look at the sky.]**

> And now... we wait. This is the weird part of twilight — you do ninety percent of the work, and then you stand around watching the sky for twenty minutes. But when it turns, it turns fast.

---

title: Twilight Masterclass
text:
Twilight Masterclass › 10. Outro / what's next  *(10:30–11:00)*

**[ON CAMERA, light starting to warm.]**

> So that's the setup — and like I said, this is where the shot is actually won. The location's scouted, the home's prepped and glowing, my hero's locked on the tripod. We are *ready*.

> In the next video, the light turns and we shoot it for real. You're going to watch me work this window live. Let's go catch it.

**[CUT TO: REM v2 outro card.]**

---
---

title: Twilight Masterclass
section: 1. Recap + where we are in the light  *(0:00–0:45)*
text:
Twilight Masterclass › 1. Recap + where we are in the light  *(0:00–0:45)*

**[CUT IN on the sky now turning — warm horizon, blue building above. Jacob at the tripod, energy up.]**

> Alright — look at that sky. It's happening. The sun's just dropped, the color's coming in, and the lights are starting to pop against it.

> If you watched the last video, everything's already done — house is prepped, hero's locked on the tripod. So now it's pure execution. Let me show you exactly what I'm doing as this light moves, because we've only got a few minutes of the really good stuff.

---

title: Twilight Masterclass
section: 2. Camera settings for a clean single exposure  *(0:45–2:15)*
text:
Twilight Masterclass › 2. Camera settings for a clean single exposure  *(0:45–2:15)*

**[Over-the-shoulder on the camera screen / settings dial.]**

> Let's lock in settings. Four things.

> **ISO — keep it low.** I'm at 100. We're on a tripod, so I don't need to crank ISO for light, and low ISO keeps the file clean — no noise in that beautiful sky.

> **Aperture — f/8 to f/11.** That's the sharp zone for most lenses, and it gives me front-to-back depth so the whole house is crisp. Bonus: at those apertures, points of light like the pathway lights turn into little starbursts. Looks great.

> **Shutter — this is my exposure lever.** Because ISO and aperture are locked for quality, I control brightness with shutter speed. Right now that might be half a second; in ten minutes as it gets darker it might be four, five, six seconds. The tripod is what makes that possible.

> **White balance — I set it manually and lock it.** I don't let the camera guess and shift on me between frames. I want my windows warm and my sky cool and blue, and I'll dial that in and leave it consistent.

> RAW, manual mode, locked white balance. That's the recipe.

---

title: Twilight Masterclass
section: 3. The single-exposure philosophy (why I don't bracket)  *(2:15–3:30)*
text:
Twilight Masterclass › 3. The single-exposure philosophy (why I don't bracket)  *(2:15–3:30)*

**[ON CAMERA next to the tripod.]**

> Now here's something that might surprise you. A lot of people bracket twilights — they shoot a bunch of exposures and blend them, or they shoot the sky separately and replace it later. I don't. I shoot **one single exposure.**

> Why? Because if you nail the timing, you don't need to. When the sky and the windows are balanced, one frame holds all of it — the color in the sky *and* the glow in the house. No blending, no fake sky, no Photoshop gymnastics.

> That's the whole reason we obsess over timing. Get the moment right in camera, and the photo's basically already made. A sky replacement always looks a little... off. Real light, caught at the real moment, just looks *right*. People can feel the difference even if they can't name it.

> So my job right now isn't to capture five versions to fix later. It's to catch the *one* perfect moment. Which means I have to work the window.

---

title: Twilight Masterclass
text:
Twilight Masterclass › 4. Shooting the hero ground angle  *(3:30–5:00)*

**[Jacob fires the hero. Show the frame on the back of the camera.]**

> So here's my hero — the wide, straight-on shot on the tilt-shift. Verticals dead straight, the home standing tall, sky breathing up top, windows glowing.

**[Fire a frame, check it.]**

> And there's the first real one. Look at that. But watch — I'm not done, because that sky is going to keep getting better for the next few minutes and then it's going to die. So I'm going to keep shooting this same frame as the light drops.

**[Adjust shutter, fire again.]**

> See, it got a touch darker, so I bumped my shutter from one second to two to keep the exposure even. I'll do that every minute or so — re-check, adjust shutter, fire again. I'm building a little sequence of the exact same composition at slightly different moments, so when I get to the edit I can pick the single best one.

---

title: Twilight Masterclass
section: 5. Working the window — harvesting the light  *(5:00–6:30)*
text:
Twilight Masterclass › 5. Working the window — harvesting the light  *(5:00–6:30)*

**[Faster-paced. Jacob moving between his pre-scouted angles, firing, checking.]**

> This is what I mean by working the window. The hero's getting its sequence, so now I move — fast — through the other angles I scouted in daylight. Three-quarter angle here... fire. Back of the house with the pool... fire.

**[Glance at sky, then back.]**

> And I keep one eye on the sky the entire time. The second I see peak — that perfect balance — I run back to the hero and get it, because the hero is the shot that matters most.

> This is exactly why we scouted everything earlier. I'm not thinking about composition right now. I'm not adjusting tripod legs and framing from scratch. Every position is already decided. I'm just moving, leveling, adjusting shutter, and clicking. Pure harvest. The thinking's done — now it's hustle.

---

title: Twilight Masterclass
text:
Twilight Masterclass › 6. Balancing the interior glow  *(6:30–7:45)*

**[Back of camera, zoom into the windows in the frame.]**

> Let's talk about the glow itself, because this is what makes a twilight feel premium.

> When I expose this frame, I'm exposing for the *sky* first — I want that color rich and not blown out. And because we turned on every light in that house, the windows naturally come up warm and glowing at that same exposure. That contrast — cool blue sky, warm glowing glass — that's the entire emotional punch of the photo.

> What I'm watching for is windows that go pure white and lose all detail. A little of that is fine, it reads as "bright and inviting." Too much and it looks like a blown-out mess. If a window's screaming, I know I can pull a touch of that back in the edit — but I'd rather get it close right here.

> Warm inside, cool outside, balanced exposure. If I've got that on the back of the camera, I know I've got a winner.

---

title: Twilight Masterclass
text:
Twilight Masterclass › 7. Creative & detail angles (24–70 handheld)  *(7:45–8:45)*

**[Jacob pulls the camera off the tripod, switches to the 24–70, shooting handheld.]**

> Once I've got my hero locked, if there's still a little color left, I'll grab some creative angles handheld on the 24 to 70.

**[Shooting through a plant / toward the pool.]**

> Shooting through some landscaping in the foreground for depth. A reflection of the lit house in the pool — that's a gorgeous detail shot. A tighter frame on the entry glowing. These are the supporting images that round out a twilight set and give the agent options.

> Quick note — once I'm off the tripod and handheld in this low light, I have to bump my ISO and open my aperture to get a fast enough shutter so it's not blurry. So these are a slightly different settings game than the locked-off hero. But they're bonus shots — the hero on the tripod is always the priority.

---

title: Twilight Masterclass
text:
Twilight Masterclass › 8. The drone twilight  *(8:45–9:45)*

**[B-ROLL: drone lifting off, then the aerial twilight on the controller screen.]**

> If the property earns it — and the light's still hanging on — I'll put the drone up for an elevated hero.

> An aerial twilight is a flex shot. It shows the whole estate, the grounds, the pool, the home glowing in context, the colored sky stretching out behind it. For a big luxury listing, that can be the cover image.

> Same principles apply up here — low ISO, expose for the sky, let the house glow. The drone window is even tighter because it's the last thing I do, so I get it up, get my frames quick, and bring it home before the color's gone.

---

title: Twilight Masterclass
section: 9. Knowing when you've got it / when to stop  *(9:45–10:30)*
text:
Twilight Masterclass › 9. Knowing when you've got it / when to stop  *(9:45–10:30)*

**[Sky noticeably darker now. Jacob relaxed, reviewing shots on the camera.]**

> And... that's basically it. Look at the sky now — the color's almost gone, it's going flat and dark. That's my cue. Once it looks like night, I'm done. Anything I shoot now just looks like a dark photo, and we've already got the good stuff.

**[Scroll through frames on the back of the camera.]**

> Let me show you what we got. There's the hero sequence — and right there, that frame, that's the one. Sky's perfect, windows are glowing, it's balanced. The three-quarter. The pool reflection. The drone. That's a complete twilight set, and it took us about fifteen minutes of actual shooting.

> Fifteen minutes of shooting, an hour of setup. That ratio is twilight in a nutshell.

---

title: Twilight Masterclass
section: 10. Wrap — what we're taking into the edit  *(10:30–11:00)*
text:
Twilight Masterclass › 10. Wrap — what we're taking into the edit  *(10:30–11:00)*

**[ON CAMERA.]**

> So that's the shoot. We caught the window, we got the hero, and we've got a clean single exposure that's holding everything we need.

> But we're not done — because a great twilight is *made* twice. Once in the camera, and once in the edit. In the last video, I'm taking this exact hero frame back to the desk and editing it start to finish, so you see the whole journey, camera to final.

> I'll see you at the computer.

**[CUT TO: REM v2 outro card.]**

---
---

title: Twilight Masterclass
section: 1. Intro — the goal of the edit  *(0:00–0:45)*
text:
Twilight Masterclass › 1. Intro — the goal of the edit  *(0:00–0:45)*

**[SCREEN RECORDING begins — the RAW twilight open in Lightroom. Facecam in corner.]**

> Welcome to the edit. This is the hero frame we shot in the last video, straight out of camera, untouched.

> Here's my entire philosophy for editing a twilight in one sentence: **enhance what's there, don't fake what isn't.** We caught real light at the real moment. My job now is to bring it up to its full potential — richer sky, warmer glow, cleaner image — not to invent a photo that never existed. That's why it's going to look believable, because it *is* real. Let's build it.

---

title: Twilight Masterclass
text:
Twilight Masterclass › 2. Selecting the frame  *(0:45–1:45)*

**[Scrolling the hero sequence in the Lightroom filmstrip.]**

> First, I pick my frame. Remember I shot a sequence of the same hero as the light dropped — so here they all are, slightly different moments.

> I'm looking for the one where the sky color is richest *and* the windows are glowing but not totally blown out. This one's a touch early, sky's a little bright. This one's a touch late, getting dark. This one — right here — that's the balance. That's our money frame. Everything from here is on this single file.

---

title: Twilight Masterclass
text:
Twilight Masterclass › 3. Lightroom base — global balance  *(1:45–3:30)*

**[Working the Basic panel in Lightroom.]**

> I start every edit on a base preset that basically does nothing — it's a clean, neutral starting point, not a one-click filter. From zero, I build.

> First, white balance. I want to push the split we talked about — keep that sky cool and blue, and let the interior lights stay warm and inviting. I'll set my temp and tint so both of those feel right at the same time.

> Then exposure and contrast to taste. I'll pull my highlights down a little to recover any window detail that's getting too hot. Lift the shadows gently so the dark areas of the house still have some life. Maybe a touch of vibrance to make that sky sing — but easy, I don't want it cartoonish.

> Because it was a longer exposure, I'll add a little noise reduction to keep the sky smooth. This LR pass is the foundation — get it balanced and clean here, then we go deeper.

---

title: Twilight Masterclass
section: 4. The split: warm windows, cool sky  *(3:30–4:45)*
text:
Twilight Masterclass › 4. The split: warm windows, cool sky  *(3:30–4:45)*

**[HSL / color mixer panel, then graduated adjustments.]**

> Let me go a level deeper on that warm-cool split, because it's the soul of the image.

> In the color mixer I can fine-tune individual colors — deepen the blues in the sky, keep the oranges and yellows in the windows warm and rich. I'm pushing the two ends apart just slightly so the contrast between cool sky and warm home is intentional, not accidental.

> If part of the sky needs help, I'll drop a graduated filter from the top to deepen the color up there while leaving the house alone. Little moves. The goal is for someone to look at this and *feel* cozy and aspirational, without ever being able to point at what I did.

---

title: Twilight Masterclass
text:
Twilight Masterclass › 5. Into Photoshop — fire, glow & light  *(4:45–6:30)*

**[Right-click → Edit in Photoshop. Photoshop opens.]**

> Now I take it into Photoshop for the things Lightroom can't do. This is where a good twilight becomes a great one.

> First — fire. If there's a fireplace or a fire feature, I've got an action that adds realistic fire, and I use the same signature flame every time so agents start to recognize my work. Fire at twilight is pure magic, it draws the eye instantly.

**[Dodging window glow.]**

> Next, I enhance the glow. I'll gently dodge — brighten — the warm light spilling from the windows and the landscape lighting, so the house feels like it's genuinely lit from within. Subtle. I'm amplifying real light, not painting in fake light.

---

title: Twilight Masterclass
text:
Twilight Masterclass › 6. Cleanup — clutter, distractions, fixes  *(6:30–7:45)*

**[Using the Remove tool / spot work in Photoshop.]**

> While I'm in here, I clean up anything that pulls the eye the wrong way. This is where I'm glad I scouted in daylight — there's not much, but there's always something.

> A stray power line across the sky — gone. A little reflection or a hot spot on a window I want to calm down. A sprinkler head, a hose bib, a smudge on the glass. The Remove tool makes this fast. None of this is "faking" the home — it's the same cleanup a stylist does in person, just done in post.

> Clean image, no distractions, eye goes exactly where I want it: the glowing home against that sky.

---

title: Twilight Masterclass
text:
Twilight Masterclass › 7. The cinematic color + finish  *(7:45–9:00)*

**[Lumenzia panel / color grade, then sharpening.]**

> Now the finish that gives my work that filmic, high-end feel. I'll add a subtle cinematic color grade — just a touch of green into the image, around six to eight percent, using Lumenzia. It's barely perceptible, but it's the difference between "nice photo" and "this looks like a film still."

**[Sharpen.]**

> Then I sharpen — with a mask so I'm sharpening the architecture and the details, not the smooth sky. I don't want a crunchy, noisy sky; I want crisp edges on the home and soft, clean color above it.

> That's my Photoshop work. I'll flatten and send it right back to Lightroom for the final polish.

---

title: Twilight Masterclass
section: 8. Back to Lightroom — warm/matte finish, perspective, crop  *(9:00–10:30)*
text:
Twilight Masterclass › 8. Back to Lightroom — warm/matte finish, perspective, crop  *(9:00–10:30)*

**[Back in Lightroom for finishing.]**

> Back in Lightroom for the final pass — this is my signature finish.

> I go for a warm, slightly matte look. I'll pull dehaze and clarity *down* a touch — counterintuitive, I know, but it gives the image that soft, expensive, glowing feel instead of harsh and over-processed. Then I lift the very bottom of the tone curve just slightly for that gentle matte black. Premium, calm, inviting.

> Perspective correction — one last check that my verticals are perfectly straight. The tilt-shift did most of this in camera, but I'll confirm it here.

> And finally the crop. I'll crop to my final ratio, clean up the edges, and frame it so the home and the sky are perfectly balanced. Done.

---

title: Twilight Masterclass
text:
Twilight Masterclass › 9. Export for MLS / print / social  *(10:30–11:15)*

**[Export dialog in Lightroom.]**

> Last step — export. And how I export depends on where it's going.

> For the MLS and the agent's marketing, I export full resolution, high quality — they may print this big, put it on a brochure, a billboard, who knows. Give them the best file.

> For social, I'll do a second export sized and sharpened for Instagram so it looks crisp on a phone. Same image, two purposes. And I keep my full-res master so I've always got the best version archived.

---

title: Twilight Masterclass
text:
Twilight Masterclass › 10. Before & after reveal + course wrap  *(11:15–12:00)*

**[Toggle the before/after split — RAW vs. final. Hold on it.]**

> And here it is. This is what we started with, straight out of camera... and this is the final.

**[Hold the reveal.]**

> Same photo. Same real light, the moment we caught on location. We didn't fake it — we enhanced it. Richer sky, warmer glow, clean and cinematic. *That's* the money shot.

**[Facecam, warm close.]**

> So that's the entire twilight process — from showing up in daylight and prepping the house, to working that twenty-minute window, to bringing the hero to life at the desk. This is the exact thing I get paid premium money for, and now it's yours.

> Go shoot one. Seriously — find a listing, check your sun times, show up early, and catch that window. It'll be rough the first time and incredible by the third. Tag me when you do — I want to see it.

> I'll see you in the next one.

**[CUT TO: REM v2 outro card — logo, "REM ACADEMY," CTA.]**

---

**⚠️ Font gotcha (fixed 8/10, in BOTH builders + render scripts):** a `<link>`ed fonts_local.css with `font-display:swap` makes Chrome `--print-to-pdf` snapshot **fallback fonts** (Helvetica/Georgia/Menlo) — all 7 PDFs shipped that way once. The fix (keep it): **inline** the fonts css into `<style>` with `swap→block` (the `FONTS` var in both build scripts) + `--virtual-time-budget=10000` on the Chrome call. Verify any new PDF with `strings x.pdf | grep -oiE "SpaceGrotesk|Helvetica"` — SpaceGrotesk/CrimsonPro/HankenGrotesk/JetBrainsMono must appear; Helvetica/Menlo only as rare single-glyph subsets.

title: Photo Critique Bot
text:
Photo Critique Bot

REM Academy **Photo Critique Bot** — a paid, gated asset (access for REM Academy members + Jacob's 1-on-1 students) that critiques uploaded real estate photos and returns a scored scorecard + ranked fixes. Started 2026-06-17.

**Locked decisions (from Jacob, 2026-06-17):**
- Purpose: **paid** REM Academy asset (not free); ties into the course funnel. Branded with the REM Design System (Paid) (dark teal `#182c2d`, emerald `#1aa861`, EB Garamond).
- Scope: **in-camera + edit**.
- Output: **scorecard** (per-category /10) + **ranked fixes** tagged reshoot/post/polish.
- Benchmark: **neutral professional industry standard** (not Jacob's personal look) — engine can be swapped to a "shoot-like-JG" coach later if he wants.
- Scale: **1–10** (no floor — honest full range; changed from the earlier 5–10 floor on 2026-06-17 per Jacob). Anchors: 7 = solid MLS-ready, 9–10 = portfolio, 3–4 = weak, 1–2 = unusable.
- Cardinal rule: **grade the photo, not the property** — the home's niceness/grandeur is out of the photographer's control and must not move the score. And **don't invent faults** — never assert distortion/tilt/cast you can't clearly see (Jacob caught a wrong "ceiling is bowing" call).

**The engine (core IP):** `~/JG Terminal/REM Photo Critique Bot/critique-engine.md` — a deployment-agnostic system prompt. Classifies the photo, grades 10 categories (verticals/horizontals, perspective & angle, focal length/distortion, camera height/position, composition, staging & frame hygiene, exposure/dynamic range, WB/color, light quality/direction, edit craft), weights in-camera fundamentals heaviest, severity tiers reshoot / post / polish. Built from Photo Process & Gear + industry research (16–24mm sweet spot, ~47" chest-height default, 1-pt/2-pt perspective, verticals plumb).

**Deployment plan:** test in-chat first (Jacob uploads photos → Claude runs the engine to calibrate scoring/voice) → recommend a **branded web app** (his domain, Claude API on his key, real login/paywall) as the real paid product, since Projects/artifacts can't truly gate paid access. A branded shareable Claude artifact is the quick interim if he wants a members link fast.

**Status (2026-06-17):** ✅ **LIVE at https://bot.remacademy.co** — built, deployed (GitHub → Vercel), custom domain connected, scorecard bug fixed, scale set to a straight 1–10, and a **gallery mode** added (critique up to 35 photos from one property as a single set — overall rating + consistency read + set-level fixes, no per-photo scorecard). Full architecture, deploy chain, engine rules, calibration history, technical lessons, and how-to-update/train are in the handbook → **Critique Bot Build Log** (read that first when resuming). **2026-08-10:** gate is now two-tier — paid code (`REM_FOUNDER_50`) + free-community code **`REMFREE`** (for the free Skool, per Round 2 Strategy funnel); each critique logs `tier: member|free` in Vercel logs. Current state = git commit `d4013f0`; repo local path = `~/JG Terminal/REM Academy/Website/rem-critique-bot/`.

title: Photo Process & Gear
text:
Photo Process & Gear

Jacob's end-to-end real estate photo process, captured from his 2026-06-16 mentoring call ([member] (Mentee)). Full detail + live edit walkthrough in `~/Downloads/[member]-1on1-2026-06-16/summary.md` (and `transcript.txt`).

**Gear (minimal-kit philosophy — least gear for best quality, even sacrificing ~3%):**
- Flash: simple Godox speedlight (said "8600", likely V860-class). Doesn't need the ~$900 strobe; extra power (e.g. [member]'s AD400 Pro / "8400 Pro") only matters for ~1 full-power shot per shoot in big homes.
- Modifiers: beauty dish (Bowens) for bouncing off white ceilings; shoot-through umbrella (often handheld) for non-white walls / flashing from outside — get the smaller one for interiors; reflective/bounce umbrella for softer light when there's time. No lantern/ball softbox (too slow).
- Trigger: SmallRig Bluetooth remote (~$20) on a ~3-sec self-timer; never the phone (disconnects).
- Lenses: 24mm tilt-shift (has Rokinon; wants Canon TS-E + a 17mm for interiors + a 50mm), 24–70 (handheld), 12–24 (ultra-wide room-connection shots).

**Shooting:** Pre-visualize before firing. Per shot capture: window/ambient frame, interior ambient, a "flat" frame (flash from behind camera, ~45° off white ceiling, for fixes), and targeted bounce-flash frames. **Core principle: nail the lighting in ONE frame (~90% of final), then build fixes off it.** Closer flash-to-wall = harder/less spread; farther = softer/more even. Keep light direction physically plausible and consistent between connected rooms. Bounce off white/near-white surfaces when possible. Often a single flash frame is enough. Camera on Flash white balance; keep some ambient in flash frames (don't black out) even if it blows the window (mask it back).

**Editing (Lightroom → Photoshop → Lightroom):** Base "Mike Kelly" preset that does nothing. In LR: fix window frame (blues down, sky pops), ambient frame (desaturate blues/aqua/purple/magenta, kill yellows), sync ONE white balance across all flash frames. In PS (Open as Layers): reverse order (ambient bottom), best-light flash on top + a nearby "fix" frame, auto-align, black mask + soft brush ~14% flow to paint light in, toggle layers to check competing shadows/mirror reflections, mask the window back in (Object Select W / polygon lasso), ambient layer via "ambient blend luminosity" at ~25–40%, "add fire" action on fireplaces, a reusable signature "fire" so agents recognize his work, Remove tool for clutter, Lumenzia cinematic green ~6–8%, sharpen mask ~35–45. Back in LR: warm/matte finish (drop dehaze/clarity, lift curve), perspective correction, crop to hide align gaps. Organize: red label (6) + pick (P); red persists library-wide; catalog by quarter.

**Exteriors/twilights:** all single-exposure; grounding shots on 24 TS, 24–70 handheld for creative angles, drone when light's good; sky replacement rarely needed if shot at the right time; twilights single-exposure on a tripod.

See Pricing & Positioning for how he charges, and Jacob Profile.

title: Pricing & Positioning
text:
Pricing & Positioning

Jacob's pricing as of 2026-06-16 (he noted he intends to **raise** these — booking volume justifies it). Source: [member] (Mentee) call, `~/Downloads/[member]-1on1-2026-06-16/summary.md`.

**Positioning strategy:** establish first (post great flash work, optionally low intro price to build buzz) → raise prices for NEW clients over time → bring existing clients up gradually. Manufacture demand so price is secondary "within reason" (Louis Vuitton / Saint Laurent analogy). Target luxury = every agent doing $1M+ listings; pitch "stay at the top, don't get caught by young hungry agents." Also target builders/architects/large brokerages for volume.

text:
SOP 00 — Start Here › 🚦 START HERE — Framed by JG VA Playbook

**Welcome.** This folder is your operating manual. Each SOP is a step-by-step recipe for one task. Read this page first, then use the others as you need them.

*Owner: Jacob Guthrie · Last updated: 2026-06-23*

title: SOP 00 — Start Here
text:
SOP 00 — Start Here › What Framed by JG does

Luxury real estate photography & videography in the Santa Barbara / Montecito area. A "job" = one property shoot. Your role is to run the operations around each job so Jacob can stay behind the camera and on growth.

title: SOP 00 — Start Here
text:
SOP 00 — Start Here › The 3 golden rules

1. **Money & client messages get Jacob's OK first.** Never send an invoice or email to a client without Jacob confirming — until he tells you otherwise. (Claude is built to pause for this.)
2. **Don't guess.** If a price, address, email, or which-file is unclear, ask Jacob. A wrong invoice or wrong gallery is worse than a 30-second question.
3. **Invoicing lives in Stripe. Bookkeeping lives in QuickBooks.** Never create invoices in QuickBooks — Jacob's bookkeeper handles that. (See SOP 01.)

title: SOP 00 — Start Here
text:
SOP 00 — Start Here › How you work with Claude

Most of these tasks are powered by **Claude skills** — you tell Claude what you want in plain English and the skill does the multi-step work. Skills are grouped under **"Framed by JG"** in Claude's Customize → Skills tab.

- **To invoice:** just say *"Invoice [client] for [address] — [line items]."* → the `framed-invoicing` skill runs.
- More skills are being built (Pixieset delivery, Vimeo uploads). Until a skill exists, use the **manual SOP** in this folder.
- Rule of thumb: **"Run the skill → it does X."** If you're unsure whether a skill exists for something, ask Claude "is there a skill for this?"

title: SOP 00 — Start Here
section: The job lifecycle (how a shoot flows)
text:
SOP 00 — Start Here › The job lifecycle (how a shoot flows)

```
1. BOOK      → lead comes in (form) ............... Monday: Bookings — Unconfirmed
2. CONFIRM   → client says yes + date set ......... Monday: move to Bookings — WIP
3. SHOOT     → Jacob shoots the property
4. EDIT      → photos/video edited (Dropbox) ...... editors work in WIP
5. DELIVER   → build Pixieset gallery + Vimeo ..... SOP 02
6. INVOICE   → send the Stripe invoice ............ SOP 01  → Monday: Invoicing
7. GET PAID  → client pays in Stripe .............. SOP 04
8. RELEASE   → turn off the gallery download pin .. SOP 04
```

title: SOP 01 — Invoicing a Client
text:
SOP 01 — Invoicing a Client › SOP 01 — Invoicing a Client

**Goal:** Send a client a Stripe invoice for a completed shoot and log it on Monday.
*Owner: Jacob · Last updated: 2026-06-23 · Status: ✅ Automated (skill: `framed-by-jg:framed-invoicing`)*

---

title: SOP 01 — Invoicing a Client
text:
SOP 01 — Invoicing a Client › ⚠️ Read first

- **Invoices are created in STRIPE only — never QuickBooks.** QuickBooks is bookkeeping; the bookkeeper pulls Stripe in monthly. A QuickBooks invoice would double-count revenue.
- **Get Jacob's OK before the invoice actually sends.** Claude builds it as a draft and shows you the total first — confirm with Jacob, then send.

title: SOP 01 — Invoicing a Client
text:
SOP 01 — Invoicing a Client › When to use

A job is delivered (or being delivered) and needs to be billed. On Monday it's usually in **Bookings — WIP → Delivered**, ready to move to the **Invoicing** board.

title: SOP 01 — Invoicing a Client
text:
SOP 01 — Invoicing a Client › What you need

1. Client / agent **name + email**
2. **Property address** (this becomes the invoice title)
3. **Shoot date**
4. **Line items** — what to charge (e.g. "Photography $950, Twilight $350, Cinematic Film $1,950"). If you only know square footage, Claude can price it from the table below.

title: SOP 01 — Invoicing a Client
section: The fast way (with Claude) — do this
text:
SOP 01 — Invoicing a Client › The fast way (with Claude) — do this

1. Tell Claude, in plain English:
   > *"Invoice The Ebbin Group, [email], [address], shot 6/22 — Exterior Photography $350, due today."*
2. Claude will:
   - find or create the client in Stripe,
   - build the invoice as a **draft** (property address as the title, Jacob's Shoot Terms footer auto-applied),
   - show you a **summary with the total**.
3. **Confirm the total with Jacob.** When he says go, tell Claude **"send it."**
4. Claude emails the invoice (with payment link) and logs it to the **Monday Invoicing board** under "📤 Invoice Sent — Awaiting Payment."
5. Give Jacob the confirmation (invoice link + total).

title: SOP 01 — Invoicing a Client
section: The manual way (fallback, if Claude is unavailable)
text:
SOP 01 — Invoicing a Client › The manual way (fallback, if Claude is unavailable)

In the Stripe dashboard → **Invoices → Create**:
1. **Customer:** search the client's email; if new, add them (name + email).
2. **Description / title:** the property address (e.g. "[address]").
3. **Line items:** add each service + price (see pricing below).
4. **Footer:** Jacob's Shoot Terms (auto-applies on his account).
5. **Due date:** per Jacob's terms — usually **due on receipt / within 7 days**.
6. Review → **Send**. Then add a card to the Monday Invoicing board manually (Client, Email, Amount, Stripe link, status = Invoice Sent).

title: SOP 01 — Invoicing a Client
section: Pricing reference (confirm with Jacob — he raises these over time)
text:
SOP 01 — Invoicing a Client › Pricing reference (confirm with Jacob — he raises these over time)

- **Photography by sq ft:** 0–2k = $800 · 2k–3k = $950 · 3k–4k = $1,200 · +$150 per extra 1,000 sq ft (cap ~$1,800)
- **Add-ons:** Twilight $350 · Verticals/Vignettes $350
- **Cinematic Listing Film:** ~$1,500–$1,950
- **Builders / commercial:** $4,500/day + licensing
- *Exterior-only or custom scopes: ask Jacob for the price — don't assume.*

title: SOP 01 — Invoicing a Client
text:
SOP 01 — Invoicing a Client › Done when

✅ Client received the invoice · ✅ A card exists on the Monday Invoicing board with the Stripe link and status **📤 Invoice Sent**.

title: SOP 01 — Invoicing a Client
text:
SOP 01 — Invoicing a Client › If something's wrong

- **Wrong amount / wants changes before sending?** Tell Claude to update or "delete the draft" (drafts vanish cleanly).
- **Already sent and wrong?** Don't delete — tell Jacob; a sent invoice must be voided/credited in Stripe.
- **Client not found / duplicate clients?** Ask Jacob which is correct before sending.

➡️ Next: once they pay, see **SOP 04 — Payment Follow-Up & Releasing Galleries.**

title: SOP 02 — Pixieset Gallery & Delivery
text:
SOP 02 — Pixieset Gallery & Delivery › When to use

The photos (and video, if any) for a shoot are edited and ready to send to the client.

title: SOP 02 — Pixieset Gallery & Delivery
section: Step A — Find the files in Dropbox
text:
SOP 02 — Pixieset Gallery & Delivery › Step A — Find the files in Dropbox

- **Photos:** `Dropbox → Jacob Guthrie → "<address> (Final Edits)"` (e.g. *320 W Sola St (Final Edits)*). The edited JPGs sit loose in that folder.
  - **Only upload images** (`.jpg`/`.jpeg`/`.png`). Skip any PDFs or other files (invoices sometimes sit in there).
- **Video:** usually in a separate **"Finished Videos"** folder, not the shoot folder.
- **⚠️ "Online only" files:** if a folder looks empty, the files are cloud-only. In Finder, right-click the folder → **"Make Available Offline"**, wait for it to download, then continue.
- If you can't find the right folder or there are duplicates (e.g. "(2)"), **ask Jacob** which is final.

title: SOP 02 — Pixieset Gallery & Delivery
text:
SOP 02 — Pixieset Gallery & Delivery › Step B — Create the gallery

1. In Pixieset → **Client Gallery → New Collection**.
2. **Name it the full property address**, e.g. `[address]`. (Nothing else — just the address.)

title: SOP 02 — Pixieset Gallery & Delivery
section: Step C — Build the photo sets
text:
SOP 02 — Pixieset Gallery & Delivery › Step C — Build the photo sets

In the **Photos** tab:
1. **Rename the default set "Photos" → "Images."** All the edited photos go here.
2. Add more sets **only as needed**, named exactly:
   - **Films** — if there's video
   - **Revised Images** — if there are revised photos
   - **Revised Films** — if there are revised videos
   - **Floor Plans** — if there's a floor plan
3. Upload each file type into its matching set.

title: SOP 02 — Pixieset Gallery & Delivery
section: Step D — Set the cover (paintbrush icon, top-right)
text:
SOP 02 — Pixieset Gallery & Delivery › Step D — Set the cover (paintbrush icon, top-right)

1. Click the **🖌 Cover** icon on the right.
2. Set the **cover photo to a hero shot** of the property (the best exterior/front).
3. Change the **Typography to "Serif."**

title: SOP 02 — Pixieset Gallery & Delivery
text:
SOP 02 — Pixieset Gallery & Delivery › Step E — Settings tab

Set these exactly:
1. **Favorite →** turn **Favoriting OFF**
2. **Store →** turn **Store OFF**
3. **Download →** set **Web Size Downloads to 2048 px** (not the default 1024)
4. **Download Pin →** keep the **pin ON** for now. ⛔ Downloads stay locked **until the client pays in Stripe** — then you turn the pin OFF (see SOP 04).

title: SOP 02 — Pixieset Gallery & Delivery
section: Step F — Video to Vimeo (if there's a film)
text:
SOP 02 — Pixieset Gallery & Delivery › Step F — Video to Vimeo (if there's a film)

Upload the video to **Vimeo**, name it the property address, set privacy to unlisted, and copy the share link. *(A Vimeo upload skill is coming; for now do it manually.)* Add the Vimeo link into the gallery and/or include it in the delivery email.

title: SOP 02 — Pixieset Gallery & Delivery
section: Step G — Deliver to the client
text:
SOP 02 — Pixieset Gallery & Delivery › Step G — Deliver to the client

Send the client the **gallery link** (and **Vimeo link** if video). **Run the delivery email past Jacob before sending** (golden rule #1). Then log the gallery link on the Monday **Bookings — WIP** card (Final Gallery field) and mark it **Delivered**.

title: SOP 02 — Pixieset Gallery & Delivery
text:
SOP 02 — Pixieset Gallery & Delivery › Done when

✅ Gallery named by address · ✅ sets correct (Images + any Films/Revised/Floor Plans) · ✅ cover = hero shot, Serif · ✅ Favoriting off, Store off, downloads 2048, **pin ON** · ✅ video on Vimeo · ✅ client delivered + Monday updated.

title: SOP 02 — Pixieset Gallery & Delivery
text:
SOP 02 — Pixieset Gallery & Delivery › If something's wrong

- Missing/blurry hero shot for the cover → ask Jacob which image to use.
- Not sure if a set is needed → only create sets you actually have files for.
- **Never turn the download pin off before payment** unless Jacob says so.

title: SOP 03 — Monday Booking Pipeline
text:
SOP 03 — Monday Booking Pipeline › The flow

```
Booking form → card lands on BOOKINGS — UNCONFIRMED (New/Unconfirmed group)
        │  (you send a quote → status "Quote Sent")
        ▼
Client confirms + shoot date set → MOVE the card to BOOKINGS — WIP (To Shoot)
        │  (shot → In Editing → Under Review → Delivered)
        ▼
Marked DELIVERED → MOVE to INVOICING (To Invoice) → send Stripe invoice (SOP 01)
```
When a card **moves** between boards, the shared fields (Client/Agent, Shoot Date, Deliverables, Shoot Brief) carry over; prices/notes do **not** travel to WIP (keeps money away from editors).

title: SOP 03 — Monday Booking Pipeline
section: What you do at each stage
text:
SOP 03 — Monday Booking Pipeline › What you do at each stage

1. **New lead (Unconfirmed):** confirm details, send a quote → set Booking Status to **💬 Quote Sent**.
2. **Confirmed:** once the client says yes and a date is set, move the card to **WIP → To Shoot**.
3. **In production (WIP):** keep the status current (To Shoot → In Editing → Under Review → Delivered). Assign the Photo/Video Editor. Drop the raw files link and, later, the Final Gallery link on the card.
4. **Delivered:** move the card to **Invoicing → To Invoice**, then run **SOP 01**.

title: SOP 03 — Monday Booking Pipeline

title: SOP 04 — Payment Follow-Up & Gallery Release
text:
SOP 04 — Payment Follow-Up & Gallery Release › Where you watch

The **Monday Invoicing board** ([18418306410](https://jacobtguthries-team.monday.com/boards/18418306410)):
- **Payment Status** column: 🔴 Unpaid / 📤 Invoice Sent / ✅ Paid
- **Overdue?** column auto-shows **⚠️ OVERDUE** when an unpaid invoice passes its Due Date — these are your follow-up list.

title: SOP 04 — Payment Follow-Up & Gallery Release
text:
SOP 04 — Payment Follow-Up & Gallery Release › Daily check

1. Open the Invoicing board, sort/scan for **⚠️ OVERDUE** and **📤 Invoice Sent**.
2. Cross-check anything that looks paid against Stripe.

title: SOP 04 — Payment Follow-Up & Gallery Release
section: Following up (suggested cadence — confirm with Jacob)
text:
SOP 04 — Payment Follow-Up & Gallery Release › Following up (suggested cadence — confirm with Jacob)

Jacob's terms are **payment due on booking/receipt**, so don't let these sit:
- **On/just after due date:** friendly reminder with the payment link.
- **+3 days:** second nudge.
- **+7 days:** flag to Jacob to step in.
- **Always run the reminder wording past Jacob** before sending (golden rule #1). Keep it warm and professional — these are repeat luxury agents.

title: SOP 04 — Payment Follow-Up & Gallery Release
text:
SOP 04 — Payment Follow-Up & Gallery Release › When a client pays ✅

1. In Stripe, confirm the invoice shows **Paid**.
2. On the Monday Invoicing card: set **Payment Status → ✅ Paid** and move it to the **✅ Paid** group.
3. **Release the gallery:** open that property's gallery in Pixieset → **Settings → Download** → turn the **Download Pin OFF**. The client can now download. (See SOP 02 for where this setting lives.)
4. If the delivery email didn't already go out, confirm the client has the gallery (and Vimeo) link.

> 🔜 **Coming soon:** a `release-gallery` skill will check Stripe for "Paid" and flip the Pixieset pin off for you. Until then, do step 3 by hand.

title: SOP 04 — Payment Follow-Up & Gallery Release
text:
SOP 04 — Payment Follow-Up & Gallery Release › Done when

✅ Invoice marked Paid on Monday (in the Paid group) · ✅ gallery download pin turned OFF · ✅ client can download.

title: SOP 04 — Payment Follow-Up & Gallery Release
text:
SOP 04 — Payment Follow-Up & Gallery Release › If something's wrong

- **Partial payment / payment plan?** Don't release downloads — check with Jacob.
- **Client says they paid but Stripe doesn't show it?** Don't release; ask Jacob to verify before unlocking.
- **Never turn the pin off before confirming payment in Stripe.**

title: Portfolio Page Conventions
text:
Portfolio Page Conventions

Standing conventions for new portfolio pages on Framed Website (repo `~/JG Terminal/Framed by JG/website`, data in `src/data/projects.json`):

**Gallery order** (Jacob's fixed sequence — he expects this without being asked):
1. Twilight hero shots (3–4) at the very front (when twilights exist)
2. Front exterior daytime
3. Interiors, in shoot order
4. Back exterior daytime (pool/patio side)
5. Back exterior twilight
6. Remaining drone shots (day aerials first, twilight aerials last)

For simpler shoots with no twilights: front exterior → interiors → back exterior.

**Why:** He corrected the default filename order on 1149 Canyon Crossing ("You need to reorder, remember?") and dictated the full twilight sequence for [address]

**How to apply:** Classify every image by previewing it (320px sips previews, batch-read). Name processed files sequentially (`NNN-slug.jpg`) so order is encoded. Cover = strongest twilight/front hero.

**Resolution:** default script is 1600px; when Jacob says keep shots "very high-res" use `sips -Z 2560 -s formatOptions 85` (~1MB/img). Corrections batches from the editor (`*_1.jpg` WeTransfer files) replace their originals.

**Hero (added 7/30):** every project page opens with an 86vh photo hero — cover image with location/address/blurb/credits overlaid, `<Nav overlay />`, cover filtered out of the gallery. The hero `<Image>` is `unoptimized` (never recompressed), so export the COVER file at 3840px q88 from the camera original whenever a source exists. Site-wide widow rule: `text-wrap: pretty/balance` in globals.css + `noWidows()` (src/lib/projects.ts) glues the last 4 words of project copy — no text block may end in a short hanging line; min 4 words on the last line.

**Blurb voice:** first-person, warm, 2–4 sentences, ends with a personal note ("One of my favorite shoots to date"); headline is a short italic phrase. Credits are freeform lowercase strings ("shot for X", "shot in collaboration with Y", "built by Z") — rendered uppercase by CSS.

**Node on this Mac:** `~/.local/node/bin` (no system node/brew; launch.json's `jgwebsite` config already uses it).

I'm so confident in my work that I know when I'm talking to someone that has no idea what I do. like, they're going to see my work, and they are immediately going to want to talk to me again. And I'm not saying that because I'm cocky, I'm saying that because it's happened, probably. at least 40 times now, right? To a point where it's statistically significant enough that I can say that it's probably going to happen again. So, when you… again, this is why I talk about pricing, positioning, you know, the way you position and market your brand, and the way your work looks, because you have to do less work. You have to spend less time on those terrible phone calls with terrible agents, right? They just book you. And… Because they want that work. It's just a product that they want, right? I don't… I don't go to a luxury fashion store and ask them what all the materials are made out of, and where the factories are. No, I just… I got sold because everybody has it, and it looks really fucking sick, and I go in the store, and I know exactly what I want, and I buy it, right? That's their exact model, right? That's how they make tons of money. So it's the same way for me, where it's like… and I'm… I literally am dealing with this right now. This guy, I went to scout a property. which I never do, actually, by the way. And I agreed to do it, because, you know, like, I don't know, this guy just wanted me to, and I did it. And and he… and he had no idea what my work looked like. Well, and I sent him my form beforehand, by the way, and I don't think he looked at it, because he didn't know… he had no idea what the pricing was like. I sent it to him after, and he goes, whoa, what's his pricing? Sent him a link to my website, hey, check out my work, and he goes, great, can we do it on Friday? Right? Like… like, so that's what I'm saying, is like, when your work speaks for itself, when you set your brand up in a certain way, and when you talk to someone with confidence, you know, you have the golden trifecta of, this person is not… they're not questioning whether or not they want to book you. For them, it's just literally only a matter of the cost, but the cost becomes justified when they see your work. So… Yeah, I mean… I mean, admittedly, I didn't even handle that perfectly. Like, it's obviously a little bit more of an awkward position when you're on a call and, like, you know.

title: Skool post: The twilight shot IS the listing. Here's how I shoot mine.
cite: Skool, The twilight shot IS the listing. Here's how I shoot mine. (2026-08-11)
text:
Skool post (2026-08-11): The twilight shot IS the listing. Here's how I shoot mine.

Five things I do on every twilight, after 1,000+ homes:

1. True dusk, not sunset. The money window opens ~15–20 minutes after the sun is gone — when the sky finally balances with the interior lights. Early = washed out. Late = black.

2. Every light in the house ON before I set up. Walk the whole property first. One black window in a shot will haunt you.

3. One hero angle. I'd rather have one perfect composition than six okay ones. Front elevation, slightly wide, verticals straight.

4. One clean exposure. My twilight is a single-exposure shot, not a 5-bracket HDR sandwich — protect the highlights in the windows and let the sky be a sky.

5. The warm/cool contrast is the shot. Tungsten glow against a blue-hour sky is why twilights sell. Don't white-balance the soul out of it.

The full workflow, on a real $18,500,000 property, linked below.

— Jacob

The Audit · Step One

## Your real hourly rate.

01

### Revenue, last 90 days, divided by three
Not your best month. The average. Pull it from Stripe or your bank, not your memory.

02

### Hours, all of them
Shooting, driving, editing or QC, uploading, invoicing, texting agents. Most people undercount by about a third, so add it back.

03

### Divide
$6,000 a month across 160 hours is $37.50 an hour. $20,000 across 240 hours is $83. $2,000 across 60 is $33.

$ 0

0

title: Cohort Two Call 1: The Audit

text:
Cohort Two Call 1: The Audit › slide 6

The Audit · Step Two

## Three numbers per shoot.

01 · AVERAGE ORDER VALUE

### What a booking pays
Every add-on included, averaged across your last 20 invoices. Not your top package. What people actually buy.

02 · HOURS PER SHOOT

### Door to delivered
Drive there, shoot, drive back, edit or QC, upload, deliver, invoice. For most of you it's five to seven hours, not two.

03 · SHOOTS PER MONTH

### Volume
The real count from the last 90 days. This is the number the client engine moves later. Today we just write it down.

AOV divided by hours per shoot is your real hourly. Everything we do for 60 days moves one of these three numbers. Nothing else.

title: Cohort Two Call 1: The Audit

The Audit · Step Three

## Price. Volume. Time.

LEVER 01

### Price
Raise the average order: tiers, add-ons, luxury positioning. The fastest money in the room, and it needs zero new clients.

LEVER 02

### Volume
More shoots: the weekly client engine, referrals, the office presentation. Slower, compounding, and it's what fills a $30K month.

LEVER 03

### Time
Fewer hours per shoot: an editor, AI, the booking system, a second shooter. This is how the $40K person gets to $100K without dying.

You pull one lever first. Pull all three at once and you pull none of them.

The Premise

## Your price is a decision.
Your market is an excuse.

title: Cohort Two Call 2: The Repricing Lab
section: slide 4: Three tiers, priced by the property.
cite: Cohort Two Call 2: The Repricing Lab, slide 4
text:
Cohort Two Call 2: The Repricing Lab › slide 4

The Structure · One Slide, Then We Build

## Three tiers, priced by the property.

TIER 1
$800
Under 2,500 sq ft. Editorial stills, 25 to 30 frames, twilight included. The floor, not the average.

TIER 2 · THE ONE THEY PICK
$950
2,500 to 4,000 sq ft. Same standard, more rooms, the frame they'll use for the sign.

TIER 3
$1,200 +
4,000 sq ft and up, plus $150 per additional 1,000. Add-ons: video, aerial, floor plan, socials, each $350 and up.

Your numbers will differ by market. The shape won't. Square footage sets the tier, add-ons build the invoice, and there is no custom quote.

## A price sheet you believe in.

At $2K to $5K a month the problem is not that your prices are low. It's that you don't have any. You have a range you say out loud and adjust based on the face they make.

01

### Set the floor from the audit
Your real hourly times seven hours per shoot is the least a booking can pay before it costs you money.

02

### Three tiers above that floor
Tier one is the floor plus margin. Tier two is the one you want. Tier three exists so tier two looks reasonable.

03

### Say it 20 times this week
The first ten times you'll flinch. By twenty it's just the price. That's the entire skill.

The Email · Written Live, Sent Live

## Four lines. No apology.

SUBJECT: NEW PRICING STARTING NOVEMBER 1

- Line 1: Thank you, specifically. One listing you shot for them, by address.

- Line 2: Starting November 1, pricing is by the property. Tier one, two, three, with numbers.

- Line 3: Everything booked before then stays at the current rate.

- Line 4: Here's the booking link. Talk soon.

WHAT'S NOT IN IT

- No "I know this is a lot."
- No reasons list. One reason at most, and it's the standard of the work, never your costs.
- No "let me know if that works for you."
- No discount for the people you like.

One of you sends this on the call. To a real client. We read the reply next Monday.

"What do you usually get for that?" Let them describe it. Then: "That's a different product. Here's what mine does for your listing." Never argue the $200.

02

Yes, at tier one. You never remove from a tier. You never build a fourth option on the phone.

03

Trade scope, never price. Fewer frames, no twilight, same rate per frame. The number on the invoice doesn't move.

A member plays the agent. You answer live. We run each one twice.

The Premise

## Nobody hires the luxury photographer.
They hire the one who looks like it.

Your work might already be luxury-grade. Your website, your grid, your reply speed and your price page are telling agents something different. Positioning is not a mindset. It's twelve checkable things.

title: Cohort Two Call 3: The Luxury Audit
cite: Cohort Two Call 3: The Luxury Audit, slide 4
text:
Cohort Two Call 3: The Luxury Audit › slide 4

The 12 Signals · 1 to 4

## What they see first.

01

### The first screen
One hero image, what you shoot, where. If they scroll to learn what you do, you lost.

02

### Your worst photo
They judge you by it, not your best. Find it and delete it. Today.

03

### Curation
Thirty images, not three hundred. Only the work you want to be hired for.

04

### The price signal
"Starting at" on the site, or nothing and a booking form. Never "contact for rates" with no anchor.

title: Cohort Two Call 3: The Luxury Audit
cite: Cohort Two Call 3: The Luxury Audit, slide 5
text:
Cohort Two Call 3: The Luxury Audit › slide 5

The 12 Signals · 5 to 8

## What they see next.

05

### Reply speed and shape
Under an hour, and the reply is three options, never a single number.

06

### The Instagram grid
Nine tiles is a sales page. Luxury interiors, one twilight, one of you working. No memes, no dog.

07

### One reel that proves the standard
Pinned. The listing, the process, the finished frames. Thirty seconds.

08

### Google and reviews
A Business Profile with your best ten photos and five real reviews. Agents check.

title: Cohort Two Call 3: The Luxury Audit
cite: Cohort Two Call 3: The Luxury Audit, slide 6
text:
Cohort Two Call 3: The Luxury Audit › slide 6

The 12 Signals · 9 to 12

## What they see after.

09

### The name
A studio name or your name. Either works. "HDR" in the name says you sell HDR.

10

### The delivery
A gallery page with your name on it, not a Dropbox link. The delivery is the second sales pitch.

11

### On site
The kit, the truck, what you wear, how you talk to the homeowner. Agents watch this more than the photos.

12

### The follow-up
Two weeks after delivery: "How did the listing do?" Nobody does this. It's why they remember you.

Score yourself out of twelve. Under eight and your price is capped no matter how good the photos are.
