section: SLIDE 3 — "Your intro, three beats." (0:08–0:12, then INTROS 0:12–0:42)
text:
Round One Call 01 notes: Kickoff › SLIDE 3 — "Your intro, three beats." (0:08–0:12, then INTROS 0:12–0:42)

**Goal:** Make the format crystal clear, model it yourself, then run ~30 minutes of intros WITHOUT losing the room.

**Say (explain the 3 beats):**
> "Three beats, that's it. One — who you are and where you're based. Two — where you're at: brand new, shooting already, or running something bigger. Three — your #1 goal for the next 60 days. That last one matters most. Say it out loud — there's something about saying a goal in front of 40 people that makes it real. Keep it under a minute. I'll keep us moving — if I cut you off, it's love, I promise."

**Model it (go first — ~45 seconds, wristwatch it):**
> "I'll go. I'm Jacob, Santa Barbara. I've been shooting real estate since I was 18 — today it's luxury listings, $40M homes. My #1 goal for the next 60 days: every person on this call gets a real win — first client, first $10K month, whatever your version is. That's the whole reason this exists. Boom — that's the format. Under a minute."

title: Round One Call 01 notes: Kickoff
section: ⚙️ FACILITATION — the 30-minute intro block (this is the whole call, run it tight)
text:
Round One Call 01 notes: Kickoff › ⚙️ FACILITATION — the 30-minute intro block (this is the whole call, run it tight)

- **The math:** ~30 people × 60 sec = 30 min. You have ZERO slack. 45–60 sec each is the target.
- **Call on people yourself — never ask "who wants to go next?"** (that silence kills momentum). Go down the participant list, or bounce intentionally: "Sarah, you're up. Then Mike."
- **While each person talks: WRITE.** Name → column (NEW / SHOOTING / SCALING) + their goal in 3 words. This becomes slide 4.
- **React in ONE sentence, not a conversation.** "Love it — first paid client, that's happening." Then immediately: "Next up—". If you give everyone 60 seconds of reaction you double the block and die at 90 minutes.
- **Batch your bigger reflections every 5–6 people:** "Okay, noticing a pattern — half of you are already shooting but stuck at the same price point. Hold that thought, we're fixing exactly that Wednesday. Keep rolling — Dana, go."
- **Ramblers:** wait for the first breath and jump in warm — "Amazing — and what's the ONE goal?" (Redirecting to beat 3 is the polite scissors.)
- **Silent/shy folks:** if someone freezes, feed them the rails: "Easy mode: name, city, new or shooting, one goal."
- **Overflow valve:** if the room is 35+, at the halfway mark say: "To respect the hour — everyone drop your #1 goal in the chat too, so we capture every single one even if we run tight." (Screenshot the chat after — it's your goal ledger + Kit ammo.)
- **Halfway check (0:27):** if you're not ~15 people deep, tighten to 30 seconds: "Lightning round — name, city, goal."

**Transition (when done):** "Okay. That was the best 30 minutes this community has ever had. Let me read the room back to you." → scroll to slide 4.

---

title: Round One Call 01 notes: Kickoff
text:
Round One Call 01 notes: Kickoff › SLIDE 4 — "Three starting points. One destination." (0:42–0:47)

**Goal:** The payoff of the intros — show them you LISTENED. Read the actual map of the actual room off your notes.

**Say (structure — fill with real names/numbers from your notepad):**
> "Here's who's actually in this room. We've got about [X] of you brand new — never charged for a shoot. [Name] and [Name], that's you — you're going to move faster than you think, because you've got no bad habits to unlearn.
>
> We've got [X] of you already shooting — the work is good, the money doesn't match it yet. [Name], you said it perfectly: [quote their line]. That's a business problem, not a talent problem. That's exactly what this fixes.
>
> And we've got [X] running real operations already — [Name] with [detail]. You're here for systems, pricing, retention. You're also proof for everyone else on this call that the ceiling is real."

**Touch on:**
- The magic line: "Different starting points, same destination — a real business where agents rebook you every month."
- Common goals you heard (first client / $10K month / raise rates) — name the top 2–3 patterns. "Almost half this room said some version of [X]. Watch what happens when 40 people chase the same thing together."
- Beginners should NOT feel behind: "The beginners in this room are two modules away from where the veterans started."
- **Tie to the intake data:** "This matches your intake forms almost exactly — landing luxury clients, systems and time, pricing. That's literally why the schedule looks the way it does. Speaking of which—"

**Transition:** "—here's the frame we're all running in."

---

title: Round One Call 01 notes: Kickoff
text:
Round One Call 01 notes: Kickoff › SLIDE 5 — "July 20 → September 10." (0:47–0:50)

**Goal:** Make 8 weeks feel structured, short, and winnable. Walk the timeline dots left to right.

**Say:**
> "Sixty days. Sixteen live calls. The rhythm: one teaching call and one conversation call every week. Teaching is me — workshops, live demos, and guest masterclasses. Conversations are like tonight — photo reviews, hot-seats, Q&A, and business check-ins where we look at YOUR numbers and YOUR roadblocks."

**Touch on (point at the dots as you go — this is the v3 structure):**
- Week 1: "Wednesday — Pricing, Packaging & Positioning. Your #1 requested topic. We start with money."
- Week 2: LIVE how I shoot a property — "full shoot, flash, light, composition — start to finish"
- Week 3: first guest masterclass *(tease — details on the next slide)*
- Week 4: Landing Luxury Clients — "breaking past referrals — the #1 hurdle from your intake forms, 35 of you said it"
- Week 5: guest #2 · Week 6: LIVE how I edit — "the high-end editorial look, edit along with me"
- Week 7: guest #3 · Week 8: Systems, Delivery & Getting Your Time Back (+ AI) → the final call: wins + your 90-day plan
- "Every single call is recorded. Life happens — the replays are always in Skool."

**Transition:** "And those three guest dots — let me tell you who's actually coming, because this is the part I'm most excited about."

---

title: Round One Call 01 notes: Kickoff
text:
Round One Call 01 notes: Kickoff › SLIDE 6 — THE GUESTS (0:50–0:53) 🔥

**Goal:** The hype moment. Three named industry leaders with real topics = the "this is bigger than Jacob" proof. Sell each in ~40 seconds.

**Say:**
> "You're not just learning from me in here. I'm bringing in three people at the very top of this industry, live, just for this cohort.
>
> **Monday, August 3rd — [member].** One of the best property filmmakers in the world. His masterclass: systemizing your video workflow to create world-class films. If video feels slow, overwhelming, or inconsistent for you — this call alone is worth what you paid.
>
> **Thursday, August 20th — JT Visuals.** Industry leader, educator — and his topic is building a premium brand. How you position yourself so agents see you as THE option, not A option. That's the difference between $300 shoots and $3,000 shoots.
>
> **And Monday, August 31st — Trevor Melton.** Luxury photographer out of Palm Beach, shooting the most expensive homes in the world — and he's walking you through exactly how he approaches those properties.
>
> All three are live, you can ask them anything, and every one is recorded. Guys — rooms like this do not usually get this kind of access. Show up for these."

**Touch on:**
- Video efficiency (22 mentions) + premium positioning (24) + luxury (35) were their TOP intake asks — each guest maps to one. If it fits, say it: "Each of these was picked off your intake forms. [member] = your video answer. JT = your pricing-confidence answer. Trevor = your luxury answer."
- Note the JT date: it's a THURSDAY (Aug 20) — flag it so the "guests are Mondays" assumption doesn't bite anyone.

**Transition:** "So that's who's in the building. Here's the simple weekly rhythm so you always know where to be."

---

title: Round One Call 01 notes: Kickoff
section: SLIDE 7 — "Mondays you learn. Thursdays we talk." (0:53–0:55)
text:
Round One Call 01 notes: Kickoff › SLIDE 7 — "Mondays you learn. Thursdays we talk." (0:53–0:55)

**Goal:** Cement the cadence + make the lifetime promise land.

**Say:**
> "Simple rhythm. One call a week is input — I teach, or a guest teaches, you take. The other is output — you bring work, questions, wins, problems, and we handle them together. If you only ever come to one, come to the conversation calls — that's where YOUR business gets worked on."

**Touch on:**
- Same Zoom link every time, pinned in Skool. 5 PM PT. (This week: Mon + **Wed**.)
- Lifetime access: "Everything we record, every resource, every future update to REM — yours forever. You never pay again. That's the founding deal, and it will never exist again."
- Skool is home base: calls calendar, replays, community, resources. "If you're not posting in there yet — that changes tonight."

**Transition:** "Alright — your first assignment. It's due before Wednesday and takes ten minutes."

title: Round One Call 01 notes: Kickoff
text:
Round One Call 01 notes: Kickoff › SLIDE 8 — "Set your 60-day goal." (0:55–0:57)

**Goal:** Convert tonight's spoken goals into WRITTEN, tracked commitments.

**Say:**
> "You already said your goal out loud — that was the hard part. Now lock it in. Two things before Wednesday's call: One — fill out the kickoff questionnaire; it's how I coach you specifically instead of generically. Two — post your #1 goal in Skool. There's a thread going up tonight. Written goals get tracked; we're checking these on September 10, and I want a wall of receipts."

**Touch on (point at the example tags on screen):**
- "If yours isn't crisp yet, steal one of these: land your first paid client. Sign 3 monthly retainers. Hit your first $10K month. Double your rates."
- A good goal = specific + 60-days-sized. "'Get better at photography' is a wish. 'Three paid shoots by September 10' is a goal."
- "I read every questionnaire answer. This is a small room by design — use that."

**Transition:** "Last thing — the honest talk about who actually wins in programs like this."

---

title: Round One Call 01 notes: Kickoff
text:
Round One Call 01 notes: Kickoff › SLIDE 9 — "Show up. Shoot. Ship." (0:57–0:59)

**Goal:** Set culture. Two minutes, straight talk, warm but blunt.

**Say:**
> "Real talk for one minute. The people who win in cohorts like this do four boring things: They show up live — replays are there, but momentum lives in this room. They shoot every week — you learn this with a camera in your hands, not in your notes. They post their work — even the rough stuff, ESPECIALLY the rough stuff; the review calls only work if there's work to review. And they ask everything — no question in here is too basic. I promise the question you're scared to ask is the one six other people have."

**Touch on:**
- "Nobody in this room is judging your work. Everyone here paid to get better — you're surrounded by the safest audience your photos will ever have."

**Transition:** "That's the whole playbook. Last slide."

---

title: Round One Call 01 notes: Kickoff
text:
Round One Call 01 notes: Kickoff › SLIDE 10 — "Let's build." (0:59–1:00)

**Goal:** End on a high, exact next step, clean out.

**Say:**
> "That's night one. You're a founding member of this thing — the bar will never be this low again, and honestly, after hearing this room tonight, I think a few of you are going to blow past every goal you just said.
>
> Two things before Wednesday: questionnaire, and your goal posted in Skool.
>
> Wednesday, 5 PM, same Zoom link — pricing, packaging, and positioning. We start with money. I'll see you there. Let's build."

**Then:** stop recording, but DON'T kill the room instantly — leave it open a couple minutes. The people who linger are your hottest community members (and future testimonials). Say goodbyes by name.

title: Round One Call 02 notes: Pricing Workshop (no recording exists)
section: SLIDE 1 — "Charge what the work is worth." (0:00–0:04)
cite: Round One Call 02 notes: Pricing Workshop (no recording exists)
text:
Round One Call 02 notes: Pricing Workshop (no recording exists) › SLIDE 1 — "Charge what the work is worth." (0:00–0:04)

**Goal:** Frame the stakes. This isn't theory — they leave with a new price list.

**Say:**
> "Morning everyone — welcome to workshop one. Monday we mapped the room. Today we fix the thing most of you said was your biggest problem: pricing. Almost half the intake forms mentioned some version of 'how do I charge more.'
>
> Here's my promise for the next hour: you'll leave with my exact pricing model — the real numbers I charge — a package structure you can copy tonight, and a step-by-step way to raise your rates without losing a single client. And here's the part I need you to actually believe: **most of you can double your income without getting one bit better at photography.** Your camera isn't the problem. Your price list is."

**Touch on:**
- Housekeeping in one breath: recorded, replay in Skool, drop questions in chat as we go — "I'll take them at the end, and Aug 6 is a whole hot-seat call where we rework YOUR pricing live."
- "Have your current prices in front of you. By the end, they're changing."

**Transition:** "Let's start with the trap almost everyone in this industry is standing in."

---

title: Round One Call 02 notes: Pricing Workshop (no recording exists)
cite: Round One Call 02 notes: Pricing Workshop (no recording exists)
text:
Round One Call 02 notes: Pricing Workshop (no recording exists) › SLIDE 2 — "Booked solid. Still broke." (0:04–0:09)

**Goal:** Make them feel seen. Diagnose before prescribing.

**Say:**
> "There's a version of this business that looks successful and feels terrible. You're shooting five, six days a week. Every listing agent in town has your number. And at the end of the month there's nothing left. Booked solid — still broke. Sound familiar to anyone? Drop a 🙋 in the chat."

**Touch on (walk the three cards):**
- **The $300 Trap** — "When you compete on price, you're competing with every person who bought a camera last month. That race has no bottom — someone hungrier will always go lower. The only way to win the race to the bottom is to not enter it."
- **Hourly Math** — "If you sell time, your ceiling is your calendar. 30 shoots a month at $300 is $9K gross and a destroyed body. The math never gets better — only busier."
- **The Haggle** — "Here's the tell: if clients regularly negotiate your price, your positioning already failed. Nobody haggles at the Louis Vuitton counter. They haggle at the flea market. Which one are you presenting as?"
- Land the punchline: "None of these are talent problems. Every one is a positioning and packaging problem — which is great news, because those are fixable this week."

**Transition:** "To fix it, we have to change what you think you're selling."

---

title: Round One Call 02 notes: Pricing Workshop (no recording exists)
cite: Round One Call 02 notes: Pricing Workshop (no recording exists)
text:
Round One Call 02 notes: Pricing Workshop (no recording exists) › SLIDE 3 — THE REFRAME (0:09–0:15) ⭐ cornerstone

**Goal:** Install the single most important idea of the day: price against the commission, not the competition. Let the bar chart do the emotional work.

**Say (as the bars animate):**
> "Look at this. On a $2M listing — normal in the luxury space — the agent's side of the commission is around fifty grand. My media bill? Fifteen hundred. That's **three percent of their paycheck.** Not the home price — their PAYCHECK.
>
> You're not selling photos. You're selling the marketing that sells the house — and wins them the next house. The listing presentation they close sellers with? Your photos. The Instagram that builds their brand? Your content. And for three percent of the commission, you're the cheapest, highest-leverage line item in the entire transaction.
>
> So stop pricing against the $300 guy. **Price against the fifty thousand dollars you're helping create.**"

**Touch on:**
- Flip the fear: "You think $1,500 sounds expensive. The agent doing $2M listings doesn't. You're projecting YOUR budget onto THEIR business — stop pricing from your own wallet."
- Second-order effect: great media wins agents their NEXT listing — you're a business-development expense, not a cost.
- "When an agent says your media helped them WIN a listing appointment, price never comes up again. That's happened to me more times than I can count."

**Transition:** "Now — you can only charge like that if you're positioned like that. Let's talk positioning."

---

title: Round One Call 02 notes: Pricing Workshop (no recording exists)
cite: Round One Call 02 notes: Pricing Workshop (no recording exists)
text:
Round One Call 02 notes: Pricing Workshop (no recording exists) › SLIDE 4 — "Manufacture demand. Price becomes secondary." (0:15–0:20)

**Goal:** The LV principle — the philosophical heart of luxury pricing.

**Say:**
> "Louis Vuitton has never once justified a price to me. Saint Laurent doesn't run 'beat any competitor' deals. The brand does the arguing before you ever walk in. And here's the thing — nobody walks in and haggles. The price is just… the price. Because the demand was manufactured before the transaction started.
>
> That's the entire game: make agents want YOU specifically — the name, the look, the reliability — and price becomes secondary. Within reason, people pay whatever the thing they already decided they want costs.
>
> Your price is a story you tell about your work. $300 says 'I'm interchangeable.' $1,500 says 'this is what serious listings use.' Agents believe the story you tell them. So tell a better story."

**Touch on:**
- The paradox that breaks brains: **raising prices can increase demand** in luxury — the price IS the signal. A $2M-listing agent is suspicious of a $300 photographer; cheap feels risky at that level.
- "I've literally won clients BECAUSE I was the expensive one. Being premium filters out the clients you don't want and attracts the ones you do."

**Transition:** "Demand doesn't fall out of the sky though — you build it with three levers you control completely."

---

title: Round One Call 02 notes: Pricing Workshop (no recording exists)
cite: Round One Call 02 notes: Pricing Workshop (no recording exists)
text:
Round One Call 02 notes: Pricing Workshop (no recording exists) › SLIDE 5 — "Three levers. All yours." (0:20–0:25)

**Goal:** Make positioning practical — three things they can act on this week.

**Say (walk the cards):**
> "**Portfolio.** Your feed is your price list. Only show the work you want more of. One $2M listing outweighs thirty starter homes — because agents look at your work and think 'that's the level I'm at,' or they don't. Ruthless rule: if a photo doesn't look like the market you WANT, it comes down. Show the market you want, not the market you have.
>
> **Experience.** From first DM to final delivery, everything should feel effortless and expensive. Fast replies. Clean booking. A delivery page that looks like a magazine, not a Dropbox link. Agents talk to each other — the experience is what they describe.
>
> **Reliability.** This is the boring one that pays the most. Luxury clients pay premiums to never worry. Show up early, deliver when you said, never miss. I've kept $40M-listing clients not because I'm the world's best photographer — because in years of working together I've never once been the problem."

**Touch on:**
- Beginners: "You have no portfolio yet — good, you also have no BAD portfolio. Shoot two aspirational homes for free ON PURPOSE (a friend's nice house, an off-market favor) and launch premium from day one. Free strategically ≠ cheap publicly."
- "Notice none of these levers cost money. They cost standards."

**Transition:** "Okay — positioning set. Now the model itself. First: what you're pricing ON."

---

title: Round One Call 02 notes: Pricing Workshop (no recording exists)
section: SLIDE 6 — "Stop selling time. Sell the property." (0:25–0:29)
cite: Round One Call 02 notes: Pricing Workshop (no recording exists)
text:
Round One Call 02 notes: Pricing Workshop (no recording exists) › SLIDE 6 — "Stop selling time. Sell the property." (0:25–0:29)

**Goal:** Move them up the pricing ladder conceptually before showing the tiers.

**Say (walk the steps):**
> "There's a ladder every shooter climbs. **Hourly** — the floor. Your income is capped by your calendar and clients literally count your minutes. **Per-photo** — better, but now you're negotiating shot counts. Still commodity math. **By the property** — this is the unlock. The property itself sets the price. And **by the outcome** — premium campaigns, retained agents — that's where the $20–50K months live, and where we're headed over the next eight weeks.
>
> Today we're installing step three: pricing by the property."

**Touch on:**
- Why property-pricing is fair AND premium: bigger home = longer shoot = bigger listing = bigger marketing budget. "The price scales with their paycheck — which is exactly why nobody argues with it."
- "It also kills the 'how long will you be there' conversation forever. They're not buying your afternoon. They're buying the listing's campaign."

**Transition:** "So here's my actual model. Real numbers."

---

title: Round One Call 02 notes: Pricing Workshop (no recording exists)
section: SLIDE 7 — THE SQFT MODEL (0:29–0:36) ⭐ the meat
cite: Round One Call 02 notes: Pricing Workshop (no recording exists)
text:
Round One Call 02 notes: Pricing Workshop (no recording exists) › SLIDE 7 — THE SQFT MODEL (0:29–0:36) ⭐ the meat

**Goal:** Hand over the exact system. Go slow. This is what they screenshot.

**Say (as the bars rise):**
> "I price photos on square footage. Under 2,000 square feet — $800. Two to three thousand — $950. Three to four — $1,200. And from four thousand up it keeps scaling — roughly $150 per additional thousand square feet. That's it. That's the whole model.
>
> Why sqft? Three reasons. It's **objective** — no negotiation, the MLS tells us the number. It **scales with the listing** — the 6,000-foot house has a bigger marketing budget than the condo, automatically. And it's **quotable in ten seconds** — an agent texts me an address, I text back a number. Speed closes."

**Touch on:**
- "Your numbers don't have to be MY numbers — your market sets the level. But the STRUCTURE is universal: tiers by size, published, non-negotiable. If your market's softer, maybe you start at $500. Structure first, numbers second."
- The floor rule: "Whatever your bottom tier is — that's your minimum to touch a camera. Mine means I don't leave the house for less than $800. Decide your number this week."
- Flag honestly: "These are my current published tiers — and I'll tell you, I'm due to raise them again. When your calendar is full at a price, the price is too low. Which we'll cover in a minute."
- Optional aside: per-photo flash option exists for special cases (15-shot $600 / 20-shot $800) — "a tool, not the system."

**Transition:** "Now — the base package is just the beginning. The real invoice gets built with add-ons."

---

title: Round One Call 02 notes: Pricing Workshop (no recording exists)
cite: Round One Call 02 notes: Pricing Workshop (no recording exists)
text:
Round One Call 02 notes: Pricing Workshop (no recording exists) › SLIDE 8 — "Add-ons do the heavy lifting." (0:36–0:41)

**Goal:** Show how a $950 shoot becomes $1,650+ — the most profitable hour of the day.

**Say:**
> "**Twilight — $350.** The money shot. The cover image, the scroll-stopper, the one that makes sellers pick THAT agent next time. Twenty-five extra minutes at the end of a shoot I'm already at. **Vertical gallery — $350.** Ten to twelve reels-ready verticals of the main spaces. Agents are desperate for social content — hand it to them done.
>
> And here's the stack: $950 base plus both add-ons is $1,650. Most of my shoots take both. So my published 'starting price' says $800 — but my real average sits around fifteen hundred to two and a half thousand. **The base gets you booked. The add-ons build the invoice.**"

**Touch on:**
- Margin logic: add-ons piggyback on a shoot you're already at — no extra drive, no extra booking. Highest-margin work you'll ever do.
- Attach-rate trick: don't sell add-ons à la carte — build them into the middle and top packages (next slide) so "most agents choose them by default."
- Tease their own menu: drone, 3D/floor plans, video tiers — same principle, whatever your market wants. "Two strong add-ons beat six weak ones."

**Transition:** "Which brings us to how you PRESENT all this. Never one number — three."

---

title: Round One Call 02 notes: Pricing Workshop (no recording exists)
section: SLIDE 9 — "Never quote one number. Quote three." (0:41–0:47)
cite: Round One Call 02 notes: Pricing Workshop (no recording exists)
text:
Round One Call 02 notes: Pricing Workshop (no recording exists) › SLIDE 9 — "Never quote one number. Quote three." (0:41–0:47)

**Goal:** Install good/better/best anchoring — the packaging move that changes close rates immediately.

**Say:**
> "When you quote one number, the client's brain does one comparison: your number versus cheaper. When you quote three, the comparison becomes YOUR floor versus YOUR ceiling — and the middle suddenly looks reasonable. Same work, same client, completely different psychology.
>
> **Essential** — photos only. It exists so the next tier looks obvious. It's the floor, not the offer. **Signature** — photos, twilight, verticals. This is where seventy percent land, so price it exactly where you want to live. **Estate** — the full campaign: photo, video, drone, twilight. Three thousand plus. Some agents take it — but even when nobody does, it's doing its job: it makes Signature feel like the smart middle instead of the splurge."

**Touch on:**
- Naming matters: "Essential/Signature/Estate — not Small/Medium/Large. The words carry positioning."
- The anchor effect is real and free: "The $3K tier makes $1,650 feel modest. Without it, $1,650 IS the scary top number. Same prices — different frame."
- "Publish them. A clean pricing page or PDF says 'established business with a system.' Made-up-on-the-spot quotes say 'freelancer guessing.'"

**Transition:** "Zoom out — here's what this model turns into."

---

title: Round One Call 02 notes: Pricing Workshop (no recording exists)
section: SLIDE 10 — "The math of a premium book." (0:47–0:50)
cite: Round One Call 02 notes: Pricing Workshop (no recording exists)
text:
Round One Call 02 notes: Pricing Workshop (no recording exists) › SLIDE 10 — "The math of a premium book." (0:47–0:50)

**Goal:** The stats slide — let the count-ups land the dream with THEIR math.

**Say (as numbers count up):**
> "Three thousand plus per luxury listing. Ten agents on rotation. Each doing two, three listings a month. That's fifty thousand dollar months — recurring — off a client list that fits on one hand and a phone screen. That's my actual number, and this is the model behind it.
>
> You don't need a thousand followers or a hundred clients. You need **ten right agents priced correctly.** That's the entire business model of this course. Everything we do for the next seven weeks — the shooting, the brand, the client acquisition — is in service of that math."

**Touch on:**
- "This is my actual life, not a funnel slide. A small book of premium agents, shot on rotation, priced right."
- Connect forward: "Landing those ten agents is the Aug 10 workshop. Today is making sure that when they say yes, the yes is worth something."

**Transition:** "So who are these agents, and what are they actually paying for? Get inside their head for a second."

---

title: Round One Call 02 notes: Pricing Workshop (no recording exists)
cite: Round One Call 02 notes: Pricing Workshop (no recording exists)
text:
Round One Call 02 notes: Pricing Workshop (no recording exists) › SLIDE 11 — "They're not buying photos." (0:50–0:54)

**Goal:** Empathy slide — when they understand the buyer, the premium makes sense.

**Say (walk the steps briskly):**
> "**Certainty** — her listing presentation is Thursday. What she's buying is the guarantee it'll be perfect and on time. **Status** — your media makes HER look like the luxury agent to sellers. You're a component of her personal brand. **Turnaround** — counterintuitive one: 24 hours or less makes it feel CHEAP. Rush is what commodity shooters sell. My turnaround is two to four days — premium work takes time, and the agents who matter respect that. What she actually needs is a delivery date she can trust, not a stopwatch. And **one less problem** — top producers juggle thirty deals at once. The vendor they never have to think about is worth almost anything."

**Touch on:**
- "Notice 'beautiful photos' isn't on the list. Beautiful is table stakes at this level — the premium is paid for everything AROUND the photos."
- Practical: build your marketing language around these four — certainty beats speed ("delivered on the date promised, every time" reads premium; "24-hour turnaround!" reads budget).

**Transition:** "Alright. New model, new packages… now the scary part: how do you actually RAISE prices when you have existing clients? Carefully — like this."

---

title: Round One Call 02 notes: Pricing Workshop (no recording exists)
cite: Round One Call 02 notes: Pricing Workshop (no recording exists)
text:
Round One Call 02 notes: Pricing Workshop (no recording exists) › SLIDE 12 — "Raise rates without losing anyone." (0:54–0:58)

**Goal:** De-risk the raise — this is the playbook that gets them to actually do it.

**Say (walk the steps):**
> "**Step one: new clients first.** Your next inquiry — not your current clients, the NEXT stranger — gets quoted the new rate. Existing clients feel nothing. Risk: zero. **Step two: let a yes make it real.** The first time a stranger says yes to the new number, it stops being an experiment. Two or three yeses and that's just… your price now. **Step three: migrate the book.** Existing agents get thirty days' notice and a reason — 'I've expanded the package: new delivery experience, verticals now included, rates update on the first.' Frame it as MORE, not just more expensive. **Step four: repeat.** Every six to twelve months, ask one question: am I booked solid at this rate? If yes — raise. A full calendar is not success. A full calendar is underpricing."
>
> "This exact ladder is how I went from cheap to where I am — I've raised again and again, and the good clients never left. The only ones who leave are the ones who were only there for cheap. **Let them go. That's the positioning working.**"

**Touch on:**
- The fear is loud, the reality is quiet: "You'll lose fewer clients than you think — usually zero of the good ones."
- Rip-the-bandaid rule for the underpriced: if you're at $300 now, don't crawl to $325 — jump to the real structure and let NEW clients carry it.

**Transition:** "Last skill: what to say when someone pushes back. Because someone will — and it's fine."

---

title: Round One Call 02 notes: Pricing Workshop (no recording exists)
cite: Round One Call 02 notes: Pricing Workshop (no recording exists)
text:
Round One Call 02 notes: Pricing Workshop (no recording exists) › SLIDE 13 — "Never discount. Reframe." (0:58–1:02)

**Goal:** Arm them with scripts + kill the discount reflex forever.

**Say (walk the cards):**
> "**'You're expensive.'** — 'Compared to what it costs a listing to sit on the market? Great media is the cheapest part of the sale.' Say it calm and friendly. You're not defending — you're educating.
>
> **'The other guy charges $300.'** — 'He's selling photos. This is your listing's marketing campaign — and your brand on every listing you take.' If they still want the $300 guy, bless them — that was never your client.
>
> **And the discount trap.** The moment you discount, you've told them the price was fiction — and they'll negotiate every job forever. If you need to move on a deal, move in VALUE: 'I can't do less, but I'll include the vertical pack on this one.' Add, never subtract. The price is the price — that sentence is a positioning asset."

**Touch on:**
- Tone coaching: objections die to calm confidence, not arguments. "The first time you say 'the price is the price' and don't flinch, something changes in you AND them."
- "Losing a price-shopper is not a loss. It's the filter doing its job."

---

title: Round One Call 02 notes: Pricing Workshop (no recording exists)
cite: Round One Call 02 notes: Pricing Workshop (no recording exists)
text:
Round One Call 02 notes: Pricing Workshop (no recording exists) › SLIDE 14 — "Reprice by Friday." (1:02–1:04)

**Goal:** Concrete homework with a deadline and a review loop.

**Say:**
> "Four moves. One — build your sqft tiers: your numbers, your market, but the structure you saw today. Two — add at least two add-ons; twilight and verticals are the obvious ones. Three — the very next inquiry that comes in gets quoted the new rate. Don't wait to feel ready; the yes is what makes you ready. Four — post your full pricing in Skool by Friday. I will personally review every single one — and on the August 6th hot-seat we'll rework them live on this call.
>
> Fair warning: I'm going to push most of you HIGHER than what you post. Nobody's posted pricing yet that was too expensive."

**Transition:** "Last slide."

---

title: Round One Call 02 notes: Pricing Workshop (no recording exists)
cite: Round One Call 02 notes: Pricing Workshop (no recording exists)
text:
Round One Call 02 notes: Pricing Workshop (no recording exists) › SLIDE 15 — "Charge like it matters." (1:04–1:05)

**Goal:** Send-off + next call.

**Say:**
> "Your price is the story you tell about your work. From this morning forward, tell a better one. Pricing in Skool by Friday — I'm reading all of them.
>
> Next call is Monday, and it's a big one: I'm going over EXACTLY how I shoot photos of a property, start to finish — flash, light, composition, the whole thing. Come see how the work behind these prices actually gets made. See you Monday. Go raise your rates."

**Then → open Q&A (1:05–1:20), off-deck.** Seed it if quiet: "Someone ask me the thing you're scared to charge — let's do the math on it live." Q&A gold: have 2–3 members share their CURRENT lowest price and rebuild it out loud — instant hot-seat preview, massive value on the recording.

title: Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot
section: SLIDE 1 — "Exactly how I shoot a property." (0:00–0:04)
cite: Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot
text:
Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot › SLIDE 1 — "Exactly how I shoot a property." (0:00–0:04)

**Say:**
> "Wednesday we priced the work. Today I show you the work. This is the exact system I run on every property — the gear, the frames, the light. Nothing held back — you're going to see actual raw files from a real luxury living room on this call. And here's the promise: by the end, the photos you've seen me charge fifteen hundred, three thousand dollars for stop looking like magic and start looking like a checklist. Because that's what it is."

**Touch on:** recorded / replays in Skool · questions in chat, big Q&A at the end · "Thursday is photo reviews — what you learn today, you shoot this week, we review Thursday. That loop is the whole course."

---

title: Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot
section: SLIDE 2 — "Least gear. Best light. One frame." (0:04–0:08)
cite: Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot
text:
Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot › SLIDE 2 — "Least gear. Best light. One frame." (0:04–0:08)

**Say:**
> "Three beliefs drive everything you're about to see. One — minimal kit. I'll happily give up three percent of quality for double the speed, because speed lets me shoot more houses with more energy and total consistency. Two — pre-visualize. My biggest early mistake: popping four hundred flashes and 'figuring it out in post.' You pay for that twice — on site AND at the desk. Three — the big one — nail the lighting in ONE frame. One flash frame is ninety percent of the final photo. Everything else is repairs."

**Touch on:** "If you remember one sentence tonight: **know what you need before you fire.**"

---

title: Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot
cite: Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot
text:
Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot › SLIDE 3 — The Kit (0:08–0:14) 🎥 show-and-tell

**Do:** hold each piece up to camera as you hit it — you name the exact models live (they're deliberately not on the slide).

**Say (walk the six cards, holding gear):**
> "Body — [name yours as you hold it]. Truly the least important thing on this slide; any modern body does this job. Glass — the 24 tilt-shift is the hero: dead-straight verticals IN camera; that architectural look everyone asks about is mostly this lens. A 24–70 for handheld work, a 12–24 for the wide connection shots. Flash — a simple Godox speedlight. Notice what's NOT here: the nine-hundred-dollar strobe. Extra power matters maybe one frame per shoot. Modifiers — beauty dish for white ceilings, and this little shoot-through umbrella I literally handhold: umbrella one hand, flash the other. Trigger — a twenty-dollar SmallRig remote on a three-second timer; never your phone, phones disconnect. And the tripod — [name yours] — it's what makes the whole frame-stack system possible."

**Touch on:** kit pays for itself in ~two shoots · "buy this list, stop watching gear videos, go shoot."

---

title: Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot
section: SLIDE 4 — The Shape of a Shoot Day (0:14–0:17)
cite: Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot
text:
Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot › SLIDE 4 — The Shape of a Shoot Day (0:14–0:17)

**Say (walk the dots):**
> "A full luxury shoot with twilight: arrive around three, walk it, prep it. Interiors while the light is boring. Verticals. Exteriors when it warms up. A break to reset, then golden hour, then the twilight window. The exact times move with the season — the SHAPE never changes. You plan the entire day backwards from the ten minutes of twilight, because you can't reorder the sun."

---

title: Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot
cite: Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot
text:
Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot › SLIDE 5 — Walkthrough & Prep (0:17–0:21)

**Say:**
> "Before one frame: I walk every room. Hero angles, where the sun is, what's going to be a problem. Then prep — declutter the counters, straighten the furniture, hide the cans... and **lights OFF for interiors.** We're building the light ourselves; the mixed color from a bunch of tungsten cans fights everything we're about to do. Then the shot list: **start in the big rooms, then work through the rest of the house in order — always.** Big rooms while your energy and the light are best, and an order means you never wander a house wondering what's next."

---

title: Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot
cite: Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot
text:
Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot › SLIDE 6 — Composition Rules (0:21–0:26)

**Say (walk the steps):**
> "One — verticals dead straight, always. That's the tilt-shift doing its job, and it's half of what reads as 'professional.' Two — height: **waist-level is the industry standard**, then minor adjustments per composition and the look you want. Lower reads more dramatic; higher pulls you out of the frame — more practical, less feeling. Three — one-point versus two-point: chosen on the emotion and practicality of showcasing the property — the flow of the rooms decides. Straight-on symmetry for formal, angled when you're selling depth and connection. Four — the wides: **24mm is the desired look**, but you'll carry a small set of wider frames — sixteen to twenty-two — because clients and the MLS expect them. Shoot them, deliver them, lead with the 24s."

**Touch on:** "Composition is free — zero gear cost, and it's where most galleries die."

---

title: Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot
section: SLIDE 7 — THE FRAME SYSTEM ⭐ (0:26–0:33) — the heart
cite: Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot
text:
Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot › SLIDE 7 — THE FRAME SYSTEM ⭐ (0:26–0:33) — the heart

**Say (slow, count on fingers):**
> "Every composition, same stack. One: the WINDOW frame — exposed for the glass; the view is part of what the house costs. Two: the AMBIENT frame — the room in natural light; the mood, the base. Three: the FLAT frame — flash from behind the camera, tipped forty-five back off the white ceiling. Almost never the final — it's the parts bin: hotspots, ceilings, floors. Four: TARGETED bounce frames — flash off a ceiling here, a wall there, sculpting; ONE of these becomes the photo. And five — **artistic flash**: flash from outside the windows for that sun-pouring-in look... or nailing the whole thing in one frame, which is always the ideal.
>
> Locked tripod. Same composition. That stack, then the next composition. Every room, every house, every price point."

---

title: Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot
cite: Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot
text:
Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot › SLIDE 8 — The Raw Frames (0:33–0:38)

**Do:** walk the four raws left to right. Let them be ugly — that's the value gap on display. (Bonus: you're visibly holding the flash in the flat frame — point at yourself.)

**Say:**
> "This is that stack for real — the hero living room. The window frame: everything's dark except the glass; that's correct. The ambient: honest, murky, moody — that's the base. The flat frame — and yes, that's me in the corner holding the flash; I'm IN the frame because it doesn't matter, this layer only donates pixels. And the bounce frame — look at the light on that ceiling and wall. That's the photo hiding in there. None of these are good photos. They're ingredients."

**Touch on:** the relief moment — "Your raws are SUPPOSED to look like this."

---

title: Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot
cite: Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot
text:
Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot › SLIDE 9 — THE REVEAL (0:38–0:41) 🔥

**Do:** scroll to it and pause. Let it breathe for a few seconds before speaking.

**Say:**
> "And those four frames... become this. Same room. Same tripod position. That's the window frame giving the view, the ambient giving the mood, the flat cleaning the ceiling, the bounce doing the light. This is a delivered, magazine-grade luxury interior — from a speedlight, an umbrella, and a system. Not talent. A system. And by Thursday you're going to have run it yourself."

**Touch on:** tie to pricing — "THIS is what three thousand dollars a listing looks like. The gap between the last slide and this one is the entire business."

---

title: Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot
section: SLIDE 10 — One Frame Is The Photo (0:41–0:44)
cite: Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot
text:
Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot › SLIDE 10 — One Frame Is The Photo (0:41–0:44)

**Say (as stats count):**
> "The numbers: ninety percent of the final is ONE frame. Five to fifteen frames per composition — bigger, more complex rooms live at the top of that range. Five to ten flash pops in the big rooms — corners, mid-walls. One flash in the whole kit. If you're firing thirty frames per comp, you don't have a gear problem — you have a decision problem, and decisions are free."

---

title: Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot
cite: Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot
text:
Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot › SLIDE 11 — Flash Craft (0:44–0:50)

**Say (walk the steps):**
> "The light rules. Bounce off white — ceilings and near-white walls are giant free softboxes; off-white is fine. Distance is your softness dial — close to the surface is hard and punchy, stepped back is soft and even; same flash, different feet. Stay TRUE to direction — never paint light from somewhere it couldn't come from, and keep direction consistent between connected rooms; viewers feel it even when they can't name it. And break the rules on purpose — bare flash through a doorway or an outside window reads as sunlight. That's a three-thousand-dollar-listing move with a two-hundred-dollar flash."

---

title: Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot
cite: Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot
text:
Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot › SLIDE 12 — Before / After (0:50–0:53)

**Say:**
> "One more, because this pair is the whole pitch: the ambient straight off the card... and the delivered final. Same room, same five minutes of shooting. Everything between the left and the right is the system you just learned plus the edit — and the edit is its own full module. The gap between these two images is what agents pay for. Not the camera. The gap."

---

title: Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot
cite: Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot
text:
Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot › SLIDE 13 — The On-Site Rhythm (0:53–0:57)

**Say:**
> "How it flows: tripod locked, remote in hand, three-second timer — fire, walk into position, the flash pops right as I land. I never walk back to the camera. Umbrella in one hand, flash in the other for most bounces — no stands, no assistant. Big rooms: **five to fifteen pops** around the corners and mid-walls — you already know which ones you'll need. And watch the mirrors — mirrors, glass, glossy tile all catch the flash; angle around what you can, note what you'll mask later."

**Touch on:** demo the remote-and-walk move on camera — it's the "ohhh" moment.

---

title: Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot
cite: Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot
text:
Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot › SLIDE 14 — Small Spaces (0:57–1:01)

**Say:**
> "The rooms everyone hates. Tiny bathroom: camera back against the door, straight on — symmetry saves it; never angle at the toilet. Phone as live-view for positions your body can't occupy. No room for the umbrella? Bounce in from the hallway — catch the corner; imperfect and invisible in the final. And sometimes the answer is shooting OUT of the bathroom into the connected space — sell the flow, not the fixtures."

---

title: Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot
cite: Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot
text:
Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot › SLIDE 15 — Verticals & Vignettes (1:01–1:04)

**Say:**
> "The $350 add-on from Wednesday, on site: ten to twelve verticals of the main lifestyle spaces. Off the tripod, 24–70, moving fast — details, textures, compression. About thirty minutes, house already prepped — the most profitable half hour of the day. Sell it by what it does: agents post these the day the listing drops."

---

title: Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot
cite: Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot
text:
Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot › SLIDE 16 — Exteriors (1:04–1:07)

**Say:**
> "Outside, everything is a single exposure. Grounding shots on the tilt-shift — front, back, straight, tall. Creative angles handheld on the 24–70 — through landscaping, pool reflections, vignettes. Drone when the property and the light both earn it. And no fake skies — shoot the right hour and you rarely need one. Real light beats Photoshop weather."

---

title: Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot
cite: Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot
text:
Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot › SLIDE 17 — Twilight (1:07–1:09)

**Say:**
> "Then the sky turns and we catch the window. Single exposure, tripod, every light in the house ON — this is the one time they all come on — exposed for the sky. Ten great minutes. I'm not teaching it tonight because the ENTIRE Twilight Masterclass is already in Skool — the real shoot on a real $20M listing plus the complete edit. Watch it before your next twilight."

---

title: Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot
cite: Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot
text:
Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot › SLIDE 18 — The Delivered Set (1:09–1:11)

**Say:**
> "What goes out the door: twenty-five to forty core photos — interiors and exteriors — ten to fifteen verticals, five to ten twilights, delivered in two to four days. And remember Wednesday: 24-hour turnaround reads CHEAP — the premium promise is a delivery date they can trust. Curated, not dumped. Early on I delivered 150 photos from one shoot — way too many. Every mediocre frame dilutes your best ten. The gallery is a portfolio, not a contact sheet."

---

title: Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot
cite: Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot
text:
Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot › SLIDE 19 — Homework: Shoot The System (1:11–1:13)

**Say:**
> "This week: shoot ONE room with the frame system. Your house, a friend's — doesn't matter. Window frame, ambient, flat, bounces — nail the light in one of them. Post your raws AND your blend in Skool. Thursday's call is live photo reviews — bring these exact frames. You shoot Monday's lesson, we fix it together Thursday. That's the loop, every single week."

---

title: Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot
cite: Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot
text:
Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot › SLIDE 20 — "Light is the product." (1:13–1:15)

**Say:**
> "The whole night in one line: gear gets you there — light is what they pay for. The camera doesn't make the three-thousand-dollar listing photo. The system does. Go run it this week, post your frames, and I'll see you Thursday. Let's go shoot."

**Then Q&A.** Seeds if quiet: "Who's shot flash before — what went wrong?" · "Name a room that scares you — I'll talk through exactly how I'd light it."

---

title: Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot
cite: Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot
text:
Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot › After the call

- [ ] Replay to Skool + post the **"Shoot the System"** homework thread (the frame stack, post raws + blend)
- [ ] Pin it until Thursday
- [ ] Anyone without a flash yet → drop the minimal-kit list in the thread

title: Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot
cite: Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot
text:
Round One Call 03 notes: How I Shoot › If things go sideways

title: Round One Call 04 notes: Photo Reviews

text:
Round One Call 04 notes: Photo Reviews › 2 · Set the vocabulary (0:05–0:07)

30 seconds, so every critique tonight uses Monday's language:
> "When I critique, I'm looking through three lenses. **Composition** — verticals straight, waist-level, one-point or two-point, what's in frame. **Light** — did you nail it in one frame, is the bounce direction true, hotspots, the window. **Edit** — white balance, the warm/cool split, how the blend holds together. Three lenses, every photo. Watch how fast you start seeing it too."

title: Round One Call 04 notes: Photo Reviews
cite: Round One Call 04 notes: Photo Reviews
text:
Round One Call 04 notes: Photo Reviews › The 6-minute review protocol (per member)

1. **(30s) Their setup** — call them off mute: "What room, what were you going for, and what did you shoot — walk me through your frame stack."
2. **(1 min) Raws FIRST** — check the system before the result: window frame? ambient? flat? targeted bounces? one frame with nailed light? *(System adherence is the homework — grade the process, then the picture.)*
3. **(30s) Chat engagement** — "Chat: what's the FIRST thing you'd fix? Type it." *(Builds everyone's eye, buys you a beat to think, makes it a room not a lecture.)*
4. **(3 min) The critique — praise → gap → fix, through the three lenses.** Always in that order. Name what's genuinely working first ("your verticals are dead straight — that's the hard part"), then the biggest gap, then the exact fix ("your bounce came from camera-left but the window's camera-right — the light's lying; bounce off the right wall and it locks in").
5. **(1 min) ONE priority fix** — "If you only change one thing on the reshoot: ___." One. They can't hold five. End warm: "Post the reshoot in the thread — I want to see round two."

title: Round One Call 04 notes: Photo Reviews
cite: Round One Call 04 notes: Photo Reviews
text:
Round One Call 04 notes: Photo Reviews › Facilitation rules

- **You drive the screen.** Members talk, you click.
- **Hard timebox.** 6 minutes each — a visible timer helps. Depth for everyone beats a masterclass for one.
- **Never dogpile.** Chat critiques must come with a fix, not just a flaw. Model it once and the room follows.
- **Tie every fix back to Monday's system** — "this is exactly the flat-frame job," "this is the one-frame principle" — so the course compounds instead of scattering.
- **Note patterns as you go** (you'll read them back in section 4).

*(Likely candidates from a first flash homework: white balance drift between frames · bounce direction not matching the window · over-flashed/flat ambience · crooked verticals · windows fully blown with no mask-back.)*

Round One Call 04 notes: Photo Reviews › Contingencies

- **Only 2–3 submissions:** go deep — 10–12 min each, then LIVE re-edit one member's raw stack in Lightroom on screen (huge value, eats time gloriously).
- **Zero submissions:** never scold. Pull 3 listings off Zillow and critique the pro galleries live with the three lenses (fun + safe), then re-edit your own Monday raw stack. Close with: "Next reviews call runs on YOUR work — post this week."
- **Too many submissions:** lightning round — 3 minutes, one lens, one fix each. Anyone unparsed gets priority queue + a personal note in the thread for Aug 17.
- **A weak photo from a fragile beginner:** double the praise specificity, critique the SYSTEM not the eye ("the stack's missing the flat frame — that's why the ceiling's hot"), give the smallest possible next step.

title: Round One Call 05 notes: Beyond the Agent
cite: Round One Call 05 notes: Beyond the Agent
text:
Round One Call 05 notes: Beyond the Agent › SLIDE 1 — "Beyond the agent." (0:00–0:04)

**Say:**
> "Every workshop so far has been about the agent — pricing them, landing them, shooting for them. Tonight I want to show you the money almost every shooter in this industry leaves on the table. The same house you photographed last week? Somebody built it. Somebody designed those interiors. Somebody shaped those grounds. Every one of them needs photos of that house — and right now, most of them are getting YOURS for free. Tonight: who the other buyers are, how licensing actually works, and how one shoot gets paid for two, three, four times."

**Touch on:** recorded / replay in Skool · "this is the highest-margin topic of the entire course — nothing tonight requires you to shoot anything new."

---

title: Round One Call 05 notes: Beyond the Agent
cite: Round One Call 05 notes: Beyond the Agent
text:
Round One Call 05 notes: Beyond the Agent › SLIDE 2 — "One house. One invoice. Why?" (0:04–0:08)

**Say:**
> "Here's the blind spot. You shoot a beautiful new build, invoice the agent, done. Meanwhile — the builder saves your photos off Zillow for their website. The designer screenshots the living room for Instagram. The landscape company grabs the twilight. Your work is marketing four businesses and you invoiced one of them. That's not flattery. That's revenue leaking. And the fix isn't confrontation — it's a system."

---

title: Round One Call 05 notes: Beyond the Agent
cite: Round One Call 05 notes: Beyond the Agent
text:
Round One Call 05 notes: Beyond the Agent › SLIDE 3 — The Six Buyers (0:08–0:13)

**Say (walk the cards briskly):**
> "Builders — every project is their portfolio; they need hero imagery of everything they build, forever. Architects — their work literally only exists in photographs; images are how they win the next commission. Interior designers — the rooms are their résumé, and you're already shooting them editorially. Landscape designers — your exteriors and twilights ARE their showcase. Brokerages — brand campaigns, the biggest checks in the market; we'll come back to them. And the sleeper tier: stagers and vendors — anyone whose work appears in your frame."

**Touch on:** "Notice: none of these buyers exist without a property you were ALREADY hired to shoot. This entire market rides on work you're already doing."

---

title: Round One Call 05 notes: Beyond the Agent
section: SLIDE 4 — "Agents buy marketing. Everyone else buys portfolio." (0:13–0:17)
cite: Round One Call 05 notes: Beyond the Agent
text:
Round One Call 05 notes: Beyond the Agent › SLIDE 4 — "Agents buy marketing. Everyone else buys portfolio." (0:13–0:17)

**Say:**
> "Why do commercial buyers pay more per image than agents? Because they're buying a different thing. An agent's photos have a two-week job — sell the listing, die in escrow. A builder's photos work for YEARS. Website, proposals, award entries, social — that image earns for them every single day. Longer use, broader use, brand-level use. That's what a license prices. Same pixels — completely different value."

---

title: Round One Call 05 notes: Beyond the Agent
cite: Round One Call 05 notes: Beyond the Agent
text:
Round One Call 05 notes: Beyond the Agent › SLIDE 5 — Copyright 101 ⭐ (0:17–0:23)

**Say (slow down — this reframes their whole career):**
> "Here's the part nobody teaches. The moment you press the shutter — you own that image. Copyright is yours by default. You don't apply for it, nobody grants it. Which means: the agent never bought your photos. They bought a LICENSE — to market the listing. That's the scope. It was never 'everyone connected to this house uses these forever.'
>
> So the builder, the designer, the stager — separate use means separate license means separate invoice. Politely. Professionally. Always. And if the builder's website is running your photos free right now — that's not a compliment, that's an unsent invoice. Tonight you learn to send it."

**Touch on:** tone matters — this is never adversarial; 90% of commercial buyers happily pay when asked warmly. They expect to. It's the shooters who never ask.

---

title: Round One Call 05 notes: Beyond the Agent
cite: Round One Call 05 notes: Beyond the Agent
text:
Round One Call 05 notes: Beyond the Agent › SLIDE 6 — "One shoot. Stacked invoices." (0:23–0:28)

**Say:**
> "So here's the model. The agent pays for the shoot — your normal listing package, the sqft model from workshop one. Work's made, edited, delivered. Then: the builder licenses the set — website and social rights. No new shoot, no new edit — pure margin. Then the designer licenses their rooms — smaller set, another invoice. And the upgrades print money for months: print rights, an ad campaign, an award submission — every expansion of use is a new line item on work you finished long ago."

---

title: Round One Call 05 notes: Beyond the Agent
cite: Round One Call 05 notes: Beyond the Agent
text:
Round One Call 05 notes: Beyond the Agent › SLIDE 7 — The Case Study ⭐ (0:28–0:32)

**Say (let the stats land):**
> "Real numbers, from a few weeks ago. A builder wanted the images from an estate I'd already photographed for the listing. Twenty-five images plus the film. Thirty-two fifty for digital and social rights — plus twenty-five dollars per image if they want print. And look at the last number: new shoots required — zero. The shoot was done. The edit was done. That's what this looks like in practice: found money on finished work."

**Touch on:** "And that license has an upgrade path built in — the print tier is already priced, waiting."

---

title: Round One Call 05 notes: Beyond the Agent
cite: Round One Call 05 notes: Beyond the Agent
text:
Round One Call 05 notes: Beyond the Agent › SLIDE 8 — Day Rate + Licensing (0:32–0:37)

**Say:**
> "Different scenario: the builder commissions the shoot DIRECTLY — no agent, no listing. Now the structure changes. My commercial day rate is forty-five hundred — the shoot, the craft, the day. Then licensing on top: fifty to a hundred fifty per image, priced by usage. The day rate makes the images exist; the license is what they're allowed to DO with them.
>
> Three ways to structure it: one day rate with the edit included. Shoot and edit as separate rates. Or waive the per-image fees and bundle a restricted license into the rate — cleaner for smaller clients. Pick per client. Scale the numbers to your market — but think in DAYS, not listings, the moment the client isn't an agent."

---

title: Round One Call 05 notes: Beyond the Agent
cite: Round One Call 05 notes: Beyond the Agent
text:
Round One Call 05 notes: Beyond the Agent › SLIDE 9 — The Four Price Dials (0:37–0:42)

**Say:**
> "Every license price is four dials. WHO — a two-person studio and a national builder don't pay the same; scale to the brand. WHERE — website and social is base tier; print costs more; paid ads and billboards cost the most. HOW LONG — one year, three years, perpetual; term limits create renewal revenue, which is a beautiful thing. And EXCLUSIVITY — if they want those images locked away from competitors, they're buying your right to resell, and that's a premium.
>
> You don't need a complicated rate card. You need to ask four questions and price the answers."

---

title: Round One Call 05 notes: Beyond the Agent
cite: Round One Call 05 notes: Beyond the Agent
text:
Round One Call 05 notes: Beyond the Agent › SLIDE 10 — "They're already at your shoots." (0:42–0:47)

**Say:**
> "Where do you find these buyers? You don't. You're already standing in their work. On every luxury listing, ask the agent ONE question: 'Who built this? Who designed it?' The agent knows, and the answer is a warm lead holding a budget. New-construction listings name the builder right in the MLS. Designers tag themselves on Instagram.
>
> Then the move you already know: gift two frames. After delivery, send the builder two or three shots of their work — free, no strings. Same reciprocity play as the twilight gift from the client-acquisition playbook. And time it to the launch week — they're literally watching your photos get attention in real time. Reach out while their own work is being admired."

---

title: Round One Call 05 notes: Beyond the Agent
cite: Round One Call 05 notes: Beyond the Agent
text:
Round One Call 05 notes: Beyond the Agent › SLIDE 11 — The Licensing Email (0:47–0:52)

**Do:** walk the template; tell them it's in Skool tonight.

**Say:**
> "The email. Subject: the property address — same trick as the Zillow method; it always gets opened. Then: 'I photographed [address] for the listing, and your work deserves better than screenshots. Attached are two frames — yours, no strings.' The gift. Then the offer: 'If you'd like the full set for your website and social, I license it ready-to-post — most of my builder clients are up and running within a day.'
>
> Why it works: they've ALREADY seen the images performing. You're not selling a shoot, a date, or a risk — the work exists. The two frames open the door, and 'ready within a day' makes yes the easy answer."

---

title: Round One Call 05 notes: Beyond the Agent
cite: Round One Call 05 notes: Beyond the Agent
text:
Round One Call 05 notes: Beyond the Agent › SLIDE 12 — The Paper (0:52–0:56)

**Say:**
> "Keep the paperwork boring and always written. One page: who, which images, what usage, how long, the credit line, the price. DocuSign for new commercial clients. And the operational rule: full-resolution files move AFTER signature and payment — watermarked previews until then.
>
> Best part of having it in writing: scope creep becomes friendly. 'Can we also run it in the magazine?' isn't an awkward favor — it's the print tier, already priced. The paper turns upsells into a menu instead of a confrontation."

---

title: Round One Call 05 notes: Beyond the Agent
section: SLIDE 13 — "The engine stays. This is the turbo." (0:56–1:00)
cite: Round One Call 05 notes: Beyond the Agent
text:
Round One Call 05 notes: Beyond the Agent › SLIDE 13 — "The engine stays. This is the turbo." (0:56–1:00)

**Say (the honest one):**
> "Now the straight talk, because I don't want anyone leaving tonight to go chase builders full-time. Agents are still the business. They rebook monthly, they're low-friction, they're the recurring heartbeat — everything from the pricing and client-acquisition workshops stands. Commercial work comes with more contracts, more stakeholders, slower timelines. I learned this myself — I still prefer realtors.
>
> So hold it in the right frame: agents are the engine. Licensing is the margin layer that rides on top — the extra one to three grand on shoots you were already doing. Build the engine first. Then turbo it."

---

title: Round One Call 05 notes: Beyond the Agent
cite: Round One Call 05 notes: Beyond the Agent
text:
Round One Call 05 notes: Beyond the Agent › SLIDE 14 — Brokerage Campaigns (1:00–1:03)

**Say:**
> "The third tier, briefly — brokerages. Brand films, office media, neighborhood campaigns, recruiting content. Five-figure projects live here — I've done them, and they're real. But here's the thing: you don't cold-pitch a brokerage. Their marketing director discovers you through their own agents' listings. Serve five agents at one brokerage brilliantly, and your name is already in the building. Every agent shoot is quietly an audition for the brand above them. Play the long game — it pays in campaigns."

---

title: Round One Call 05 notes: Beyond the Agent
cite: Round One Call 05 notes: Beyond the Agent
text:
Round One Call 05 notes: Beyond the Agent › SLIDE 15 — Homework (1:03–1:05)

**Say:**
> "This week, four moves. One — name the builder or designer behind your last three shoots; five minutes of looking, that's your warm list. Two — send ONE licensing email using the template; just one. Three — add a licensing line to your pricing page, so it exists as a real offer. Four — post your outreach draft in Skool.
>
> And LOOK AT THE SCHEDULE: the next call is **WEDNESDAY at ONE PM** — not Thursday, not five o'clock. It's the pricing and positioning hot-seat. Wednesday. One PM. I'll say it again in the thread."

---

title: Round One Call 05 notes: Beyond the Agent
cite: Round One Call 05 notes: Beyond the Agent
text:
Round One Call 05 notes: Beyond the Agent › SLIDE 16 — "One shoot. Every buyer." (1:05–1:06)

**Say:**
> "You already own the images. You already know who needs them. The only thing missing was the invoice — and now you know how to send it. One licensing email this week. Wednesday, 1 PM, hot-seat. Go get paid twice for work you already did."

**Then Q&A.** Seeds: "Someone name the builder on your last shoot — let's draft the email to them live." · "Want to see my actual one-page license? [screen-share the redacted agreement]" · "What would you charge a national builder vs the local two-person shop for the same 20 images? Let's price it with the dials."

Round One Call 05 notes: Beyond the Agent › If things go sideways

- **Running long:** compress 8–9 (commercial model + dials) into one pass and cut 14 to one line — protect 5–7 (copyright + model + case study) and 15 (homework + schedule flag).
- **"Won't the agent be mad I'm charging their builder?":** "The agent's license isn't diminished — they keep exactly what they paid for. You're licensing YOUR images for a DIFFERENT use to a different business. Most agents love it — it makes them look connected."
- **"My market has no luxury builders":** "Every market has builders, designers, and stagers — the tiers scale down with your market just like the sqft model. A $500 license in your market is still pure margin."
- **Copyright edge cases (work-for-hire contracts, MLS rules):** don't play lawyer — "check anything you've signed; if a contract says work-for-hire, that changes ownership. Default is you own it. When in doubt on a big deal, a one-hour attorney consult pays for itself."

Round One Call 07 notes: Landing Luxury Clients › SLIDE 2 — "The referral ceiling is real." (0:04–0:09)

**Say (walk the cards):**

Two — and this is the one nobody notices — **your network clones itself.** Referrals send you more of what you already have. $400K-listing clients know $400K-listing agents. The referral wheel keeps you exactly where you are, forever, by design. Three — 'my work will speak for itself' — to WHO? Luxury agents cannot hire someone they've never seen."

**Touch on:** "Referrals don't stop — they become the bonus on top of a machine, instead of the whole machine."

And here's what took me years to learn — you don't get on that list by being 'better.' **Availability, reliability, and trust matter more to them than better.** Their photographer flakes, their listing launches Friday — who answers the phone? That's the job you're applying for.
>
> And understand what we actually are: an extension of their business. Without media, the listing can't go to market. Their seller can literally fire them. We're not decoration — we're infrastructure. Hunt like infrastructure."

title: Round One Call 07 notes: Landing Luxury Clients

**Say (the story — tell it real):**
> "Let me tell you about my worst month. I had my ten clients, everything was comfortable, so I stopped doing outreach — why would I need it? Then all ten had a slow month at the same time. Not one — all ten. My income cut in half, in one month, and there was nothing I could do about it in that month, because pipeline you plant today feeds you in sixty days. That's the tax on comfort.
>
> So the rule is: never stop. Clients are seasons — they leave, they slow, they lose listings, none of it's personal, all of it's inevitable. Acquisition is not a phase you graduate from. Even now, at my level, the machine never turns off."

Hunters study."

text:
Round One Call 07 notes: Landing Luxury Clients › SLIDE 6 — METHOD 1: The Zillow Method ⭐ (0:23–0:30)

**Do:** if you can, LIVE demo — Zillow, county, sort newest, open a listing, find the agent, Google → brokerage page → email. Two minutes on screen makes it real.

**Say:**
> "Method one — I call it the Zillow Method. Tedious, unglamorous, and one of the best things I've ever done for my business, entirely from a desk. Zillow, your whole county — go wider than you think, it multiplies the listings. Sort by newest. Set a minimum price so you only see listings you'd actually want. Open a listing, grab the agent's name, Google them, find their brokerage or personal site, get their direct email.
>
> Then the email — next slide — with THEIR listing address as the subject. Twenty a day. Once you're quick it's fifteen minutes. And the follow-up: seven days later, one line — 'Hey, just checking on this.' That's the whole system. It works because of what's on the next slide."

title: Round One Call 07 notes: Landing Luxury Clients
cite: Round One Call 07 notes: Landing Luxury Clients
text:
Round One Call 07 notes: Landing Luxury Clients › SLIDE 7 — The Email (0:30–0:36)

**Do:** walk the template line by line. Tell them it'll be in Skool tonight.

**Say:**
> "Subject line: the listing address. That's the entire trick. An agent will open an email with their newest listing's address in the subject basically 100% of the time — it looks like business about THEIR deal. Then: one genuine compliment about the listing — real, specific, not flattery. Who you are, locally — agents work with locals. The offer: you'd love to earn their business, with a first-time offer if you're comfortable giving one. Portfolio and Instagram links — because the second they finish reading, they're checking both. And an easy out: call, text, or email.
>
> Here's the mindset: most won't reply. **None of them forget.** You're not trying to close from one email — you're installing yourself in their memory for the day their photographer flakes. And he will."

**Touch on:** personalize every single one — name + address + the compliment. "The minute it smells like a blast, it's spam."

You now know exactly who does the volume in your market and how to reach them.

From there — personal, brief emails one at a time, maybe a foot-in-the-door offer for the very top tier. Don't mass-blast it from Mailchimp; branded blasts read as spam and die as spam.
>
> And even if nobody replies? **The list never expires.** Now you know who to follow, whose open houses to walk into, whose listings to engage with. It's your market map, forever."

Don't get caught — work with someone young and hungry who puts out the best work in the market, for YOU.' It lands because it's true — their competition IS aging into vulnerability, and you're offering to be their unfair advantage instead of their replacement's.
>
> And to the rising agent, flip it: 'Look like the number one before you are.' Same media that sells $5M listings, on their $900K listing. They level up, you level up with them — and rising stars become mega-producers who remember who believed first."

**Say:**

Feed — follow every agent on your list and engage genuinely; when your email lands, the first thing they do is check your Instagram. Your feed is the storefront; make sure the storefront matches the pitch. And in person — honestly still the best of all of it. Broker opens, open houses, market events. A ten-minute real conversation outruns fifty emails. The email gets you known; the handshake gets you hired."

title: Round One Call 07 notes: Landing Luxury Clients

**Say:**

Frame it as exclusive — 'I'd love to earn your business' — never desperate. The discount buys the audition, not the relationship. Then overdeliver violently: your best work, delivered early, with a bonus they didn't pay for. You're not profiting on shoot one — you're buying a spot in the rotation.
>
> And be honest with yourself about the clock: it took me YEARS to earn the top agents in my market. Every first shoot just starts the clock. Patience and pressure, at the same time."

**Touch on:** callback to pricing — strategic first-shoot offers ≠ public cheap prices. The rate card never changes; the door just opens.

title: 7 reel scripts
text:
7 reel scripts › Production guide (one filming session)

**Framing & look:** chest-up, eyes to the lens, your desk/studio with a clean branded background (a screen behind you showing a listing or the REM logo adds depth). Key light on your face; keep the dark-teal brand mood behind you.
**Wardrobe:** one clean, neutral outfit across all 6 (white/cream tee or quarter-zip) so the set reads as a series.
**Audio:** lav or shotgun mic — non-negotiable. Pro reels live and die on clean sound.
**Delivery:** blunt, calm, confident. Talk *to one person*. Pause between beats so the editor has clean cut points.
**Takes:** 2–3 per reel + extra **alternate hook reads** (the hook makes or breaks the reel — give options).

**B-roll to capture / pull (hand to editor):** you shooting a luxury listing (camera + gimbal), the listings themselves (twilight exteriors, interiors, the $40M homes), gear close-ups, you editing, you on a call. Reuse what you've got in your IG Post Images / listings library.

title: Cohort Two schedule post (draft v2)
text:
Cohort Two schedule post (draft v2)

TITLE: The full Cohort Two schedule: all 8 calls, October 5 to November 30

Here's the whole 60 days on one page. Save this post.

Every call is Monday at 10 AM Pacific (1 PM Eastern, noon Central, 11 AM Mountain), 90 minutes, recorded, and in the classroom under Live Call Replays the same day. One exception: call two is a FRIDAY. No call Thanksgiving week. The link for each call will be on its calendar event.

Round One taught the playbook and all sixteen replays are in the classroom. Round Two runs it on your business. Every call is a live build, a teardown, or a pitch on a real business in this room, and you leave each one with something finished. Before most calls there's one Round One replay to watch first, so we never spend live time re-teaching.

CALL 1 · MONDAY, OCTOBER 5 · THE AUDIT
Every member's numbers on screen: revenue, shoots a month, average per shoot, hours. We work out what you actually make per hour, the one lever that moves your business (price, volume, or time), and your 60-day number on a scoreboard the whole room sees. Four minutes each.
Bring: your last 90 days (revenue, shoot count, hours). The Launch Checklist post has the template.
Leave with: your real hourly rate, your lever, your number.

CALL 2 · FRIDAY, OCTOBER 9 · THE REPRICING LAB
Three real rate cards rebuilt live. The price-raise email written on the call and sent to a real client before we hang up. The cheap-market play for anyone in a $300K market. An objection lab for what existing clients say when you raise.
Watch first: replay 02, Pricing & Positioning.
Bring: your current rate card and your three most recent invoices.
Hot seats: Jackie, [member], [member], [member].
Leave with: rate card v2 and a sent email.

CALL 3 · MONDAY, OCTOBER 19 · THE LUXURY AUDIT
The 12 signals an agent checks in 60 seconds before deciding if you're the luxury option. Live teardowns of three member brands: site, portfolio, pricing page, inquiry reply, Instagram grid.
Watch first: replay 10, JT Visuals.
Bring: your website and Instagram open.
Hot seats: [member], Victor, [member].
Leave with: your score out of 12 and your top three fixes, due in seven days.
